maps.summary: The costing method works as built, and that is the problem. It prices each card against a plain unit of its tier, charges scaling to break even by turn 12, and caps growth at 0.8-3.8 SP a turn per card. Bot lobbies run at exactly the printed-stats pace it aimed for: median board 133 SP at round 12 (target 118), growth flat at 10-15 SP a round, winners' final boards 242 SP (about 17/17 a unit). By the owner's yardstick (100/100 units late) that is about 6x too small. We have no measured Battlegrounds curve to argue back. The tier curve is too flat for the real game. Tiers open at rounds 3/6/9/12/14, not the assumed 2/4/6/8/9. A plain tier 4-6 body is only 0.60-0.74 of the median unit already on the board when it arrives. Ten Battlegrounds tier 4-6 payoffs deliver a median of about 32 SP a turn; ten of ours deliver about 3. Our method would price Kalecgos at +770%. Seven of the ten pass 2 cuts were for growth over the caps, and the method has no test for "too small". On concentration, a vanilla sim under our rules confirms the owner's example: fewer, bigger bodies win by 20-28 points. But a lone carry holding 30% or more of the board loses, so "always" needs sticky units or self-scaling text. Keep the formula, geometry, firing rates, golden rule and loop guards. Replace prices anchored to V(t), break-even against a plain unit, the growth caps, the tolerance basis and the gold table.

findings.claim: The method produced the pace it targeted: a flat, printed-stats game. Boards grow by a roughly constant 10-15 SP a round and never accelerate.
findings.evidence: B3 targets about 120 SP at turn 12 (power-budget.md:735); the model assumes the rest of the lobby grows 0 SP per unit per turn (power-budget-review.md:352). Measured: lobbies/free_choice_plain.rounds.csv, attack+health per seat per round, 400 complete lobbies (scripts/lobby.py, sink.py).
findings.numbers: Median board 52 / 92 / 133 / 174 / 220 SP at rounds 6 / 9 / 12 / 16 / 20. Mean gain per round 8-16 all game. Winners' final board median 242 SP (p90 312, max 486) on 7 units, about 35 SP or 17/17 a unit. The owner's late Battlegrounds norm of 100/100 is about 200 SP a unit, roughly 6x ours. Board growth from round 4 to round 20 is about 7x.

findings.claim: The tier curve V(t) is too flat for this game. When a tier opens, its plain body is already below the board average.
findings.evidence: V(t) = 5/7/8/10/12/14, about 1.1x the Battlegrounds printed median (power-budget.md:90-104). Its assumed mean unit at each tier's turn is 5/5/6.3/7.2/9.4/10.4 (power-budget.md:120). Measured median SP per unit at the round each tier first opens (scripts/lobby.py, tierreach.py).
findings.numbers: T3: 8 against 7.6 on the board (1.05). T4: 10 against 13.5 (0.74). T5: 12 against 19.7 (0.61). T6: 14 against 23.4 (0.60). The method's assumed mean unit is about half the measured one at T4-T6.

findings.claim: The tier clock behind every 'bought when its tier opens' price is 1-5 rounds early, and the turn-12 horizon is shorter than real games.
findings.evidence: Assumed opening turns 2/4/6/8/9 (power-budget.md:119); break-even by turn 12 (power-budget.md:195, B1 at 721); model horizon turn 15 (power-budget-review.md:353). Measured first round at each tier from rounds.csv (scripts/tierreach.py), and rounds by place from players.csv.
findings.numbers: T2-T6 open at median rounds 3/6/9/12/14, and only 49% of seats ever reach T6. Winners play 19.5 rounds; the median seat is out by round 14-16. A T5 bought at round 12 gets no fights before the turn-12 break-even point.

findings.claim: Battlegrounds tier 4-6 payoffs deliver about 10x more permanent stats a turn than ours. Our method would rule nearly every one of them illegal.
findings.evidence: Table G in the detail file: 10 current-pool Battlegrounds cards from docs/research/battlegrounds/data/minions.json, and 10 pass 2 cards from Bramble-ideation-balance/content/units/*.json. Firing counts come from power-budget.md:311 (2 spells a turn at T4-6) and the costing-3 and pass2-costing rates. These are estimates, not measurements.
findings.numbers: Battlegrounds median about 32 SP a turn (range 4-140), about 3x the card's own printed body every turn. Bramble median about 3 SP a turn permanent (range 0-9), about 0.3x its body; Lollop and Laird are combat-only, at 14-28 SP a fight. Kalecgos at 40 SP a turn would be charged c(5) 2.6 x 40 = 104 SP against V(5) 12, which is +770% and 10x the T5 cap of 3.8 (power-budget.md:125, 743).

findings.claim: The costing passes cut in one direction. They remove permanent growth, compounding and quadratic synergy, and never flag a payoff as too small for the late game.
findings.evidence: pass2-costing.md:7-17 lists ten cut items: Lollop '+24 SP a turn ... six times the cap' (line 8), Mallow, Beadle, Stone Soup, Elder Ooze, Ranocchio and Stork's loop for growth, and Pie for recurring gold. Pass 1: Committee +408% 'quadratic' (costing-1.md:27), Queen of Elfland 'geometric' rebuilt to conserve stats (costing-1.md:49), Mast 'compounding' (costing-1.md:28). Pass 3: Tiddy Mun '20 SP of permanent growth a fight' (costing-3.md:77).
findings.numbers: 7 of 10 pass 2 cuts are growth over the B4 caps. The standard fixes are 'once a turn', 'once a fight', a smaller number, or moving the effect to combat-only. The method has no 'too small' test.

findings.claim: Concentration (owner's hypothesis): partly right. Under our combat rules, fewer and bigger bodies beat more and smaller ones at equal total. A single carry among small vanilla units does not, and an added buff is worth about the same spread or concentrated.
findings.evidence: Toy vanilla sim of rulebook 9.2, 9.4.2, 9.4.5, 9.5.1, 9.5.5 and 9.6 (scripts/conc_sim.py, conc_sim2.py, conc_sim3.py): 3,000-4,000 paired fights a cell on random boards, unit size 0.6-1.4x the mean. Table F in the detail file.
findings.numbers: Owner's example, 3x 10/11 against 5x 10/10: 100% wins. The same SP squeezed from 7 units onto 5: +0.20 to +0.28 win rate at boards of 42-420 SP. One carry with 20% of the board: +0.11 in F1. With 30%: -0.09 to -0.20. With 50%: -0.18 to -0.27. Adding +20% of the board's SP to one unit instead of spreading it gives 0.85x the gain, close to the method's 0.9 for a chosen target (power-budget.md:296).

findings.claim: Vanilla combat doesn't care how big the numbers are; only ratios matter. 'Too small' therefore means payoffs are too small relative to the board, flat effects are too big relative to units, and growth over the game is too slow, not that 10/10 is a worse number than 100/100.
findings.evidence: Win rate per added SP x board SP, from scripts/conc_sim2.py. It matches K = 1.9-2.1 in power-budget-review.md:139.
findings.numbers: 1.98 / 2.04 / 2.04 / 2.10 at boards of 42 / 70 / 140 / 420 SP. A Dozey-size +8/+8 is +25% of a round-7 board and moves win rate by +0.40 (conc_sim3.py, mean unit 9).

findings.claim: Absolute prices for flat effects are anchored to Battlegrounds printed boards. Our real units are bigger, so Divine Shield and similar effects are underpriced, while flat damage and Attack loss lose value as the game goes on.
findings.evidence: Divine Shield is 0.9 x A(t), with A(t) = 2.0-6.1 taken from Battlegrounds printed means (power-budget.md:114, 181). E72 damage is 0.85 x the damage dealt (power-budget.md:277). Measured mean Attack per unit (scripts/atk.py).
findings.numbers: Mean Attack per unit is 5.9 / 8.7 / 10.7 at rounds 9 / 12 / 14, against A(4) 4.0 / A(5) 4.9 / A(6) 6.1, i.e. 1.5-1.8x. The attack share is 0.36-0.46, against the default of 45-50%.

findings.claim: The gold table's own validity condition fails. Late gold buys about 1 SP a gold, not the 1.8-2.5 the gold prices assume.
findings.evidence: The gold table is read at a 2.0 sink and holds from 1.8 to 2.5 (power-budget.md:143, 358-389); costing-2.md:163 says 'Below that, re-read 4.1'. Shipped stat spells come from Bramble-ideation-balance/content/spells/*.json. Measured round-to-round board SP gain per gold spent (scripts/sink.py).
findings.numbers: Shipped spells give 1-3.3 SP a gold (Last Orders 1, Pinch of Dust 2, Beltane about 2, Boundary Stone 3), against S(t) = 5 (power-budget.md:477). Realised board gain is 1.0-1.2 SP a gold over rounds 6-11 and 0.7-0.9 from round 13 (this includes tier-ups). Banks sit at 10-12 gold from round 6 on.

findings.claim: About half of every final board is printed stats. Winners lead on goldens and higher tiers about as much as on text.
findings.evidence: Final attack+health (players.csv) against the printed A+H of the cards on the final board (cards.csv, doubled for goldens) (scripts/printed.py).
findings.numbers: Final/printed is 1.92-2.19 at every place. 1st place: printed 113.5, final 242, 3.58 goldens. 8th place: printed 57, final 112, 1.05 goldens. Text delivers about 131 SP over 19.5 rounds, about 7 SP a round for the whole board.

findings.claim: Rules-level ceilings block concentration and compounding directly, on top of the method's caps.
findings.evidence: Printed permanent-buff ceiling, with Dozey's at +12/+12 (rulebook.md:768). Ring cap +4/+4 (rulebook.md:500). Tribe bonus up to +3/+3 (rulebook.md:305). Bridge Toad permanent_buff_cap 3 and Treasurer 'up to +8/+8' (content/units). Mrs Mallow now buffs the smallest unit (pass2-costing.md:38).
findings.numbers: Even fed to the cap, Dozey ends at about 22/25. Most growth text is +1/+1, once a turn or twice a fight.

findings.claim: Item 4, keep: the parts that are ratios or counts survive a big change of scale.
findings.evidence: The cost formula (power-budget.md:162); realisation and row geometry from the rows sim (power-budget.md:551-602); firing rates (power-budget.md:303-326; costing-3 Mired deaths 0.95 a patch and Takes 0.55); the golden rule (power-budget.md:522-534); engine shapes and refresh-loop bounds (power-budget.md:442-458, content-guardrails.md:11); the whole-game bot as the arbiter (power-budget.md:680-684).
findings.numbers: Each of these holds because K x board is constant (about 2.0) in vanilla fights. Magnitudes need restating as a share of the expected board at the buy round, not in absolute SP.

findings.claim: Item 4, replace: everything anchored to the printed curve or to a plain-unit comparator.
findings.evidence: V(t)-based prices (A(t), Reborn 0.4V, Venomous 0.25V, the mean-unit table: power-budget.md:110-141); B1 break-even against a plain unit by turn 12 (power-budget.md:195-204); the B4 caps (power-budget.md:125, 743); 'linear growth only' and the E06/E08 once-a-turn rule (power-budget.md:206, 240-242); tolerance as a % of V(t) (power-budget.md:145-156); the gold table at 2.0 and flat S(t) with no board premium (power-budget.md:358-404, 466-477); B8's 4x engine limit (power-budget.md:775); the rule ceilings above.
findings.numbers: A ±25% band on V(6) = 14 is ±3.5 SP, about 2% of a 155-200 SP late board. The precision sits where outcomes don't move, and the caps sit where they do.

assumptions.assumption: Stat value is linear and additive: 1 SP is 1 Attack or Health anywhere, and a card's value is its body plus the sum of its text's SP. This prices +1/+1 to seven units the same as +7/+7 on one.
assumptions.where: power-budget.md:78, 81, 162; E01 0.9 per SP (line 235); T05 0.9 and T07 x units (lines 296-297)
assumptions.evidence_for: Vanilla sim: an added buff on one unit is worth 0.85x the same buff spread, close to the 0.9 the method uses. K x board stays about 2.0 from 42 to 420 SP.
assumptions.evidence_against: The same SP on 5 bodies beats it on 7 by +0.20 to +0.28 win rate. The 'SP' is a local slope (about 2 / board SP), so absolute prices hold at only one board size. Text that scales with a unit's own stats (E06, E08, 'gain its Attack') compounds on big units. Flat answers fall off against them.
assumptions.test: Paired fights with real card text at the measured board sizes for each round (Table A), comparing spread and concentrated delivery of the same SP.

assumptions.assumption: Attack against Health: front Attack 1.0, back Attack 0.75, Health 1.0 in either row; default split 45-50% Attack.
assumptions.evidence_for: The toy sim's row values (power-analysis.md:290-302).
assumptions.evidence_against: Real boards are Health-heavy: Attack share 0.36-0.46 (scripts/atk.py). On a carry, an Attack point's value depends on kill thresholds, which a linear rate ignores.
assumptions.test: Re-measure row values on the bot's actual boards at rounds 6, 12 and 18.

assumptions.assumption: The vanilla curve V(t) = 5/7/8/10/12/14 is linear, about 1.1x Battlegrounds' printed median, and anchors every price.
assumptions.evidence_for: It fits Battlegrounds' printed stats (power-analysis.md:41-49).
assumptions.evidence_against: Battlegrounds' printed stats price only its early game (power-analysis.md:343). In our lobbies a plain T4-T6 body is 0.60-0.74 of the median unit it joins (Table C).
assumptions.test: Set the curve from board SP per unit at the round each tier actually opens, then check that buying a tier never feels like a downgrade.

assumptions.assumption: Tiers open on turns 1/2/4/6/8/9, with the mean unit at 5/5/6.3/7.2/9.4/10.4 SP.
assumptions.evidence_for: Reproduces Battlegrounds' standard clock under Battlegrounds rules (power-budget-review.md:69).
assumptions.evidence_against: Bots open tiers at rounds 3/6/9/12/14, and only 49% reach T6. The measured mean unit is about 2x the assumed one at T4-T6.
assumptions.test: Already measured (scripts/tierreach.py). Re-read with human-like leveling once the bots' level policy is checked.

assumptions.assumption: A fairly priced scaling card breaks even with a plain unit by turn 12, bought when its tier opens; c(t) = 3.9/3.7/3.5/3.1/2.6/2.6.
assumptions.evidence_for: Derived from a committed model table (scaling_rate_caps.csv) and fairly insensitive to lobby pace (power-budget.md:203).
assumptions.evidence_against: Late payoffs don't compete with plain units; they compete with other payoffs and with the board's own units. Games run to round 14-20. The model has one player, no opponents, no triples and no tribes (power-budget-review.md:373).
assumptions.test: Rebuild the comparator on a target pace curve: a payoff is fair if, bought at its real opening round, it keeps its share of a target board.

assumptions.assumption: Growth caps per tier: 0.8/1.3/1.7/2.5/3.8 SP a turn, or 1.0/1.7/2.2/3.6/6.2 per combat firing. Above them, text must move up a tier, become conditional or be capped.
assumptions.evidence_for: Above these rates even a 1/1 body beats a plain unit by turn 12 in the model.
assumptions.evidence_against: These caps are what holds the game at printed pace. Battlegrounds' T4-T6 payoffs run 4-140 SP a turn (median 32), 3-35x over the caps (Table G). Seven of ten pass 2 cuts rest on them.
assumptions.test: Run a bot lobby with the caps lifted on 2-3 payoffs per tribe and record board SP by round, round-to-round win-rate swing and placement spread.

assumptions.assumption: Growth is linear only. Multiply and consume are once a turn and never retriggered, and multipliers never double them.
assumptions.evidence_for: Without such a rule no price holds for geometric growth.
assumptions.evidence_against: This removes compounding and the main concentration tools Battlegrounds relies on (Flaming Enforcer, Ur'zul, Tyrael). The owner names compounding as the source of Battlegrounds' scale.
assumptions.test: Separate loop guards (within a turn) from scale caps (across turns); allow cross-turn compounding and measure pace.

assumptions.assumption: Lobby pace target: printed-stats pace, about 118 SP at turn 12, with the rest of the lobby growing 0 SP per unit per turn. Its 'Battlegrounds-like' reference is 270 SP.
assumptions.evidence_for: It was met: 133 SP measured at round 12.
assumptions.evidence_against: The owner reads it as far too low (100/100 units late). The 270 figure is itself a model input, not a measurement, and no replay data exists in the repo.
assumptions.test: Measure Battlegrounds and Galaxy board stats by turn from replays or video frames (the owner's research ask), and set a target curve from them.

assumptions.assumption: Tolerance is ±15% for plain cards and ±25% for engines, as a share of V(t), with a ±1 SP floor; the golden version should come out at 2 x V(t) within that band.
assumptions.evidence_for: Owner-set on 2 Nov, and Battlegrounds tunes in ±1-2 SP steps.
assumptions.evidence_against: ±3.5 SP at T6 is about 2% of a late board, while late outcomes swing on payoffs 10x that size. All the precision goes where it matters least.
assumptions.test: Express the band as placement impact or as a share of the expected board at the buy round.

assumptions.assumption: Timing classes: combat-only effects are priced per fight, one-off recruit buffs at 0.9 per SP, and per-turn or permanent scaling with c(t) as the main risk class.
assumptions.evidence_for: Battlegrounds' scaling share rose from 6% to 32% of the pool while printed stats stayed flat (power-analysis.md:21).
assumptions.evidence_against: Charging permanence heavily pushes fixes to combat-only text (Lollop, Laird, Elder Ooze), which never compounds and gives players no lasting reward.
assumptions.test: Track the share of the pool's payoff text that is permanent, against Battlegrounds'.

assumptions.assumption: Condition discounts: tribe 0.6 or 0.3, state checks 0.7, random target 0.85, golden 0.1 or 0.25.
assumptions.evidence_for: A simple, readable default.
assumptions.evidence_against: Battlegrounds charges about 0 for tribe dependency (power-analysis.md:110). The real live rates are measurable in bot lobbies.
assumptions.test: Measure each condition's live rate by tribe and round from the bot.

assumptions.assumption: Synergy: free inputs are priced at a fixed reference, a card is priced alone, and combinations are checked only for loops. An enabler's value to other cards is not priced.
assumptions.where: power-budget.md:352, 456; pass2-costing.md:3 (priced on the board at purchase)
assumptions.evidence_for: New enablers don't re-price old cards, and loop checks catch infinites.
assumptions.evidence_against: The owner frames every card as condition, payoff and what it enables. There is no term for multiplicative synergy, and the caps forbid it.
assumptions.test: Cost tribes as packages: the board SP by round of a committed board against a mixed one.

assumptions.assumption: Economy: gold is priced at a late sink of 2.0 SP a gold (valid 1.8-2.5) with S(t) = 5, no board premium, recurring gold capped at 0/0/1/1/2/2, and engines limited to about 4x the no-engine rate.
assumptions.evidence_for: Battlegrounds' 2-4 gold-a-turn minions didn't last (power-budget.md:404).
assumptions.evidence_against: Shipped spells give 1-3.3 SP a gold, and realised growth is about 0.7-1.2 SP per gold spent, so the table is outside its own window. Battlegrounds' late board spells give 12-17 SP a gold (power-budget.md:479).
assumptions.test: Re-derive the gold value per round from the bot (SP per extra gold, by round), then pick a target late sink.

assumptions.assumption: Rule-level caps: permanent-buff ceilings (Dozey +12/+12), Ring +4/+4, tribe bonus +3/+3, Bridge Toad +3/+3.
assumptions.evidence_for: They stopped runaway lines found in the costing passes.
assumptions.evidence_against: They block exactly the concentration and compounding the owner asks for.
assumptions.test: Lift them one at a time in bot lobbies and watch placement spread and fight length.

assumptions.assumption: Payoffs should be about even with immediate power: a scaling card should not end up much stronger than a plain card.
assumptions.where: Implicit in B1 and B4 (power-budget.md:195, 205) and in every 'over, cut' verdict
assumptions.evidence_for: It makes cards fair in isolation.
assumptions.evidence_against: The owner's frame is that a payoff should outgrow the plain card, with the condition as the price (owner note 2026-11-09a, 'Condition and payoff'). In Battlegrounds, payoffs deliver about 3x their own body every turn.
assumptions.test: Owner call, then a pace target for the bot to measure.

assumptions.assumption: Flat effects keep their value across the game, priced off printed A(t) and fixed SP.
assumptions.where: power-budget.md:114, 181, 277; flat numbers in pass 2 text (Spitfire Sal 2 damage, Posset 3, Bitter 1-2, Jack Daw steals 2, Whistlers -1/-1)
assumptions.evidence_for: True on printed-pace boards.
assumptions.evidence_against: Measured Attack at rounds 9-14 is 1.5-1.8x A(t), and flat answers lose relevance as units grow, which is part of why a concentrated unit holds its stats.
assumptions.test: Price flat effects as a share of the measured unit size at the buy round.

assumptions.assumption: The late game is a short tail: horizon turn 12, model run to 15.
assumptions.evidence_for: Most decisive fights fell by turn 12 in the model.
assumptions.evidence_against: Winners play 19.5 rounds, and T6 opens at round 14.
assumptions.test: Already measured (players.csv rounds by place).

motivations.player_wants: To feel stronger every turn and to see a payoff pay off.
motivations.tension: Each capped payoff adds about 2% of the board a turn (3 SP on a 133 SP board), which players barely feel. The board grows about 10 SP a round from round 6 to the end.

motivations.system: Tier curve V(t) and the tier clock
motivations.player_wants: To tier up for better cards.
motivations.tension: A plain T5-T6 body is 0.60x the median unit already on the board when it arrives, so a tier-up only pays through text. Only 49% of seats ever reach T6.

motivations.system: Rule ceilings (permanent-buff cap, Ring cap, tribe +3/+3) and spread text (Mallow's 'smallest unit')
motivations.player_wants: A carry to build, protect and show off.
motivations.tension: The rules cap the carry, and the text spreads stats out, so few tribes offer a carry worth committing to.

motivations.system: Gold pricing at a 2.0 sink, flat S(t), recurring-gold caps
motivations.player_wants: Gold that turns into visible power, plus banking for a big turn.
motivations.tension: Late gold realises about 1 SP a gold and banks sit at 10-12, so economy cards are early-game cards whatever they cost.

motivations.player_wants: Progress they keep between fights.
motivations.tension: Combat-only payoffs reset every fight, so they never compound and leave no lasting reward.

owner_questions.question: What shape should late growth take: geometric (each payoff adds a share of the board every turn, as in Battlegrounds) or linear but much steeper?
owner_questions.why: This one choice sets c(t), the growth caps and the gold table. It is a feel target, and no measurement in our data can pick it.
owner_questions.default_answer: Geometric from about round 8. The top board should reach about 10x its round-6 size by round 14 (about 500 SP) and about 25x by round 18 (about 1,300 SP, roughly 90/90 a unit).

owner_questions.question: Should the main payoff for every tribe be permanent growth that compounds and is kept, with combat-only text kept for answers and tempo?
owner_questions.why: The costing's fixes have been moving payoffs to combat-only text (Lollop, Laird, Elder Ooze). That keeps numbers small but takes away lasting rewards.
owner_questions.default_answer: Yes. Each tribe gets at least two permanent payoffs at T4-T6 that compound. Combat-only text goes to answers, tempo and tier 1-3.

owner_questions.question: Where should compounding come from: economy (late spells and engines rising to 10-15 SP a gold, as in Battlegrounds), stat engines with gold kept flat, or both?
owner_questions.why: The owner names compounding economy as the source of Battlegrounds' scale. Our spells give 1-3 SP a gold, and the gold table is outside its valid window.
owner_questions.default_answer: Both. Spell and engine SP per gold rises with tier, to about 3x today's late rate. The recurring-gold caps stay as the snowball guard until the bot shows turn length is fine.

owner_questions.question: Should a lone carry beat an even board of the same total stats only when it has a sticky trait (cleave, damage reduction, shield, self-growth)? Or should plain bigness be enough?
owner_questions.why: In vanilla fights under our rules, fewer bigger bodies win by 20-28 points, but a carry holding 30%+ of a board loses. Where carries come from is a design choice.
owner_questions.default_answer: Only with a sticky trait. Give each tribe one sticky-carry route and put answers (poison, destroy, proportional damage) in the neutral pool.

owner_questions.question: Should high-tier printed bodies stay modest (Battlegrounds-like 10-14), with the value in text, provided every T5-T6 card delivers its tier's payoff rate within two turns of purchase?
owner_questions.why: Today a T5-T6 body is 0.6x the board average when it arrives, which makes tiering up feel like a downgrade unless the text pays at once.
owner_questions.default_answer: Yes, keep bodies modest. Test each high-tier card by its share of the expected board two turns after its real opening round, not against V(t).

owner_questions.question: Should flat numbers in answer text (2-3 damage, Bitter 1-2, -2 Attack, -1/-1) be rewritten as proportions or kills, so they still matter at 10x scale?
owner_questions.why: Flat answers fall off as units grow, and at bigger numbers they would stop answering carries.
owner_questions.default_answer: Yes for answers. Keep flat numbers only on tier 1-2 tempo cards.

maps.summary:
The pace numbers check out (400 lobbies, 3,200 players, all rows complete). The run has finished: the files are now free_choice_plain.*.csv, without the ".0" in the name. Bots first reach tiers 2-6 at rounds 3/6/9/12/14. 49% of players reach tier 6, and winners play 19.5 rounds. Battlegrounds' standard curve is 2/4/6/8/10.

Our economy does not set that pace. The bots' hand-set climb curves do. In 99-100% of the rounds where a bot at tier 2-4 didn't climb, it had the gold to. Bramble's costs allow Battlegrounds' curve. Only the 13-gold last climb holds anyone back.

Gold is flat. Everyone spends about 10 a round, whatever their tribe. Carry-over is barely used: the median most anyone banks in a game is 3. Paid refreshes peak at 9 in a turn, so the price rise after 15 never happens. Late gold adds 0.75-0.9 board stats per gold, against the 2.0 the budget prices everything on.

Every growth loop in pass 2 is linear or capped, as power-budget B4 requires. No buff on a shop card is bigger than +3/+3 per trigger. Battlegrounds prints 15 minions with +5/+5 or more, plus 45 that scale "this game" or "permanently". Winners end near 35 stats per unit. The owner's ~100/100 Battlegrounds units would be about 6x that. Our research never measured Battlegrounds boards.

On concentration: the budget treats spread stats and stacked stats as equal. Brother Bracken, the five-unit hero, is the best hero (mean place 2.70) and wins 91% of early fights. The interest hero is the worst (5.53). Tables: /tmp/claude-1000/-home-alex-code-Bramble-ideation/5369878e-e379-478d-ac97-3201f49297d2/scratchpad/fundamentals/economy-motivations.md

findings.claim: The pace figures in the brief are right.
findings.evidence: build/sim/pass2-followup/lobbies/free_choice_plain.{rounds,players}.csv (the run finished; progress.json says complete; the .0 files no longer exist). econ_pace.py: first round each player reaches each tier; tier6_turn in players.csv.
findings.numbers: First reach of tiers 2/3/4/5/6: median rounds 3/6/9/12/14 (tier 4: p25 = p75 = 9; tier 6: p25 14, p75 15, earliest 13). 1,570 of 3,200 (49.1%) reach tier 6: places 1-3 99-100%, 4th 77%, 5th 15%, 6th-8th 0-1.5%. Those who never reach it die at a median round 13. Winners play a median 19.5 rounds (p10 18, p90 21).

findings.claim: Bramble bots are 1-4 turns behind Battlegrounds' standard curve and 3-5 turns behind the timing our own power budget prices cards on.
findings.evidence: power-budget-review.md:69 gives the BG curve 2/4/6/8/10. power-budget.md:119 says tiers open on turns 1/2/4/6/8/9. economy-bounding.md:450 assumes 6-8 rounds after tier 6.
findings.numbers: Bramble 3/6/9/12/14 against BG 2/4/6/8/10: +1, +2, +3, +4, +4 turns. Tier-6 units play about 6 rounds, and only for the top half.

findings.claim: The bots' hand-set climb curves set the pace, not gold.
findings.evidence: src/core/bots/bot_level.gd:20-21 sets HARD_CURVE [4,7,9,12,14] ("tempo beats tiers in this slice"). Strategy curves live in content/bots/strategies/*.json. DECISIONS.md:538 says they were slowed by hand. econ_pace2.py checks, for each round a bot didn't climb, whether turn-start gold plus Acorn gold covered the next climb at the normal discount.
findings.numbers: Could afford the climb in non-climb rounds: tier 1: 53%, tier 2: 100%, tier 3: 99%, tier 4: 100%, tier 5: 68%. Arithmetic: BG's 2/4/6/8/10 is affordable under Bramble's costs while buying 13 units by turn 10. With no buys, tier 6 on turn 7.

findings.claim: The 13-gold last climb is the one place gold slows the climb.
findings.evidence: src/core/game_config.gd:21 (ideation-balance) sets SLICE_UPGRADE_COSTS [5,7,8,11,13]. DECISIONS.md:599 calls it provisional, tuned on one bot over 400 games.
findings.numbers: Rounds from tier 5 to tier 6: 1 round 104 players, 2 rounds 603, 3 rounds 599, 4+ 264.

findings.claim: The "tempo beats tiers" reason for the slow curves may be out of date: earlier climbers place better now. This is confounded, because bots that are ahead climb a turn early.
findings.evidence: econ_pace2.py groups players by first round at each tier. Hero table from players.csv. bot_brain.gd:262-280 moves the climb round by health and scouting.
findings.numbers: Tier 3 by round 3 (all 147 are March Hare): mean place 3.24, against 4.69 at round 6. Tier 5 at round 11: 2.94, at 12: 3.53, at 13: 4.56. March Hare is the second-best hero (3.57).

findings.claim: Gold is flat and the same for everyone. No tribe has a working gold engine.
findings.evidence: players.csv: gold_spent divided by rounds, by final tribe. rounds.csv: bank, gold_left and in-turn gain by round.
findings.numbers: Gold spent per round by final tribe: 9.69-10.10 (Hedgerow, the Acorn tribe, 9.98). Extra start-of-turn gold 0.5-2.4 a round; in-turn gold 0.4-2.1. No card raises the 10-gold income ceiling.

findings.claim: Carry-over gold is almost unused, and the interest hero is the worst hero.
findings.evidence: rounds.csv gold_left and larder. Hero table from players.csv. content/heroes/dame_farthing.json.
findings.numbers: Gold carried per turn: median 1, p90 3, max 11. Most carried in a game: median 3, p90 6. Acorn gold held: median 1, p90 5, max 22. Dame Farthing mean place 5.53 (last of 9). In balance-1.md, the Long Purse saving line wins 5.1%.

findings.claim: The rising refresh price and the 'around 20 shops' long turn never happen in play.
findings.evidence: rulebook.md:140 (3.1.2) and :232 (4.4.3). rounds.csv paid_refreshes.
findings.numbers: Paid refreshes per turn over 48,773 turns: 0 in 47%, 1 in 24%, 2 in 17%, 3 in 8%, 4+ in 4%, at most 9. The price rise at the 16th refresh never fired.

findings.claim: Late gold buys about half the stats the power budget prices every gold cost on.
findings.evidence: power-budget.md:360 prices gold on a 2.0 SP-per-gold late sink. Measured: board stats gained ÷ gold spent, summed over players (econ_pace2.py).
findings.numbers: Board stats per gold: rounds 3-6 1.32, 6-9 1.09, 9-12 1.11, 12-15 0.75, 15-20 0.91. Boards grow about 11.6 stats a round from round 9 to 20 (1.66 per unit).

findings.claim: Every compounding loop in pass 2 is linear or capped, by design. Battlegrounds and Galaxy compound far harder.
findings.evidence: content/units/*.json and content/spells/*.json (set slice, in the pool). Caps: tribe_bonus.gd:6 (+3/+3), board_upkeep.gd:8 (Ring +4/+4), Dozey permanent_buff_cap 12. power-budget.md:743-746 (growth caps; 'Linear growth only'). BG data/minions.json current solo pool. Galaxy design-notes §3. Full list of loops in the detail file, §6.
findings.numbers: Pass 2: 35 of 127 pooled cards have growth text. No buff is bigger than +3/+3 per trigger, and each grower adds about 1-8 stats a turn. Gold loops: the Acorn ladder (9 Acorns become 16 gold, +78%, capped by its sources), Farthing's interest (up to 5 a turn), Money Spider, One Swallow's homecomings. Mrs Stork is the only gold-spent counter. Tavern spells never grow. BG: 15 of 273 minions give +5/+5 or more per trigger (+10/+10 per refresh at tier 4; +8/+8 to the whole shop for 1 gold; tier 7 +20/+20 and double), and 45 texts scale 'this game', 'permanently' or 'wherever'.

findings.claim: Board scale is about 6x below the owner's Battlegrounds claim. Our research never measured Battlegrounds boards.
findings.evidence: players.csv final_attack + final_health. The owner's note of 9 Nov. power-budget-review.md:293: its 270 SP is a model guess. Indirect support: strategy-eras.md:223 counts Tyrael 'set to 50/50' as a scam.
findings.numbers: Winners' final boards: median 242 (about 35 per unit), p90 312, max 486. Median board at round 12: 133, against the budget's 118 for printed stats only and its 270 guess for Battlegrounds. The owner's ~100/100 units come to about 1,400 a board.

findings.claim: The evidence fits the owner's concentration claim, though it doesn't isolate it. Our budget assumes the opposite.
findings.evidence: power-budget.md:471 says 'no data that spread stats are worth less than stats on one unit'. Bracken numbers from players.csv and rounds.csv. DECISIONS.md:560 on Dozey.
findings.numbers: Brother Bracken (5 units or fewer: +1/+1 per tier, up to +5/+5): mean place 2.70, the best hero. He wins 91.4% of fights before round 9 with fewer recorded stats (73 against 81 at round 8; 14.6 against 11.6 per unit; about +30 from his bonus in combat). Only 13% firsts. Dozey at 96/94 was on 70-96% of final boards before his cap.

findings.claim: Triples are the biggest multiplier players actually reach.
findings.evidence: cards.csv golden flag by place.
findings.numbers: Goldens per final board: 1st 3.58, 2nd 2.87, 4th 1.71, 8th 1.05. 29.7% of all final-board units are golden.

assumptions.assumption: Late gold buys about 2.0 SP per gold, and every gold price on a unit is read at that rate.
assumptions.evidence_for: The one-player model gets 1.97-2.04 for a no-engine tier-6 player buying spells at 5 SP per gold.
assumptions.evidence_against: Bot boards gain 0.75-0.91 stats per gold from round 12 on. In economy-bounding.md, BG-style engines make 7-10 SP per gold. The owner's claim implies far more.
assumptions.test: Read SP gained per gold by tier phase from the bench rounds table on each commit. Re-run power-budget 4.1 at the measured sink.

assumptions.assumption: Stat growth must be linear and small: 0.8/1.3/1.7/2.5/3.8 SP a turn by tier. Multiply effects only once a turn and never retriggered.
assumptions.evidence_for: It stops one card from beating a plain unit outright in the one-player model, and it prevents loops.
assumptions.evidence_against: It is the opposite of the owner's compounding direction. Battlegrounds prints +10/+10-per-trigger engines and Galaxy accepts thousands. Pass 2 boards end at about 35 per unit.
assumptions.test: An owner call (question below). Then a bench arm with 2-3 uncapped 'this game' counters per tribe, measuring board scale and how long a lead lasts.

assumptions.assumption: A Tavern spell buys a flat 5 SP per gold, on purpose below Battlegrounds' 12-17 late board spells.
assumptions.evidence_for: It keeps the late sink near 2.0 so the gold prices hold.
assumptions.evidence_against: Pass-2 spells deliver 1-5 SP per gold. Last Orders, the tier-5 spell, gives 1 per gold. It caps how much late gold can change a board.
assumptions.test: Price the shop's spells per gold at a full board, then bench a +50% spell-rate arm.

assumptions.assumption: Stats are interchangeable: one SP is worth the same anywhere, and spreading them carries no discount.
assumptions.evidence_for: Simple and additive, so cards can be costed by sums.
assumptions.evidence_against: The owner's 3×10/11 against 5×10/10 example. Bracken is the top hero at 2.70 with fewer units. Dozey dominated at 96/94.
assumptions.test: Run fixed-SP fight sweeps: the same total stats on 3, 5 and 7 units, with and without cleave or damage-reduction units, through the combat engine (headless fixtures, no lobby).

assumptions.assumption: The bot data's tier pace reflects the game's economy.
assumptions.where: implicit in every pace or tier-value reading from bench data; src/core/bots/bot_level.gd:21; content/bots/strategies/*.json
assumptions.evidence_for: Curves move ±1 with health and scouting.
assumptions.evidence_against: Climbs at tiers 2-4 were affordable in 99-100% of the rounds where bots didn't climb. The curves were slowed by hand (DECISIONS.md:538). The earliest tier-6 turn anywhere is 13.
assumptions.test: A bench arm with the BG curve 2/4/6/8/10 and one with 'climb when gold allows plus one buy', compared on place and tier-6 share.

assumptions.assumption: With no timer, turns get long: most long turns see about 20 shops, so we need rising refresh prices and loop guards.
assumptions.evidence_for: The owner decided it (N8). It keeps future engines bounded.
assumptions.evidence_against: No more than 9 paid refreshes in 48,773 turns. Most turns see 0-2. The rise never fires.
assumptions.test: Track paid plus free shops per turn by tier in the bench. Re-check once compounding engines exist.

assumptions.assumption: Carry-over gold with no cap and no interest makes banking a strategy.
assumptions.evidence_for: It gives burst turns and wastes nothing. Lump buys exist (Hiring Fair, Market Stall, Last Orders).
assumptions.evidence_against: The median most a player banks in a game is 3. Dame Farthing (interest) is the worst hero at 5.53. The Long Purse wins 5.1%.
assumptions.test: A by-hand playtest, plus a bench strategy that saves toward Last Orders, Beltane Bonfire or Hiring Fair turns.

assumptions.assumption: Recurring gold is capped at 0/0/1/1/2/2 a turn by tier, one-off gold at 2/2/1/1/1/1, and nothing raises the income ceiling of 10.
assumptions.evidence_for: Battlegrounds' 2-4-gold-a-turn minions didn't last. It guards against snowballs.
assumptions.evidence_against: It keeps gold flat and equal (about 10 a round for every tribe), so gold can't drive compounding. BG lets max gold rise (Grifter, Sightseer, Snare Trapper).
assumptions.test: An owner call on where compounding lives, then bench arms with +1 max gold sources.

assumptions.assumption: The last climb costs 13 (two more than Battlegrounds).
assumptions.evidence_for: With one bot, Spend Late won 29.2% at 11 and 22.2% at 13.
assumptions.evidence_against: It was tuned on one bot. Tier 6 is now 3-4 turns later than Battlegrounds and half the lobby never sees it.
assumptions.test: Re-bench 11 against 13 under faster bot curves.

assumptions.assumption: A board of about 120 SP at turn 12 (printed stats) is the pricing pace, and 270 is 'Battlegrounds-like'.
assumptions.evidence_for: Our model reproduces it, and the bot's 133 at round 12 is close.
assumptions.evidence_against: The 270 is a guess. The owner reports BG late units over 100/100, roughly 1,400 a board.
assumptions.test: Extract real board stats by turn from Battlegrounds or Galaxy replays or videos (owner's research ask).

assumptions.assumption: Early losses should be cheap (no base damage in rounds 1-3) and greedy openings safe.
assumptions.evidence_for: Slow starts survive to the late game (balance-1.md). The three openings are level for bots.
assumptions.evidence_against: Rainy Day pays 3 gold for a loss against 2 for a win (1 + Spoils), so a loss can be worth taking. Untested by hand.
assumptions.test: Count by-hand rounds where a player gave up a fight in rounds 1-3.

motivations.player_wants: Spend it all each turn: about 3 buys and a roll.
motivations.tension: Gold is the same for everyone late (9.7-10.1 a round by tribe), so it can't be what separates players.

motivations.player_wants: Hold gold only for a lump: a discounted climb, Hiring Fair (6), Market Stall (4), Last Orders, Beltane Bonfire, Charcoal Burner.
motivations.tension: Banking costs tempo and earns nothing, except the 1-gold climb discount for each turn you wait. In practice nobody banks: the median most carried in a game is 3.

motivations.system: Buying and selling, Bought or Created
motivations.player_wants: Replace the weakest unit for 2 net gold. Keep generated units, because they sell for 0.
motivations.tension: Board slots are the scarce thing. Created-for-0 stops churn loops but also makes generated units dead money.

motivations.player_wants: Roll with the 1-2 gold left after buying, or to finish a triple.
motivations.tension: Meant to bound very long turns. It never binds: at most 9 refreshes in a turn.

motivations.player_wants: Keep a third copy or a key unit for next turn.
motivations.tension: Locks out fresh offers. With banked gold it sets up a big next turn.

motivations.system: Upgrade costs and the per-turn discount
motivations.player_wants: Wait until the climb is cheap.
motivations.tension: Tempo now against better shops later. The discount is the only built-in reward for waiting. The 13-gold last climb leaves players 2-3 rounds at tier 5.

motivations.player_wants: Climb to see more cards of your own tier (a tier-6 shop is 40% tier 6).
motivations.tension: Low-tier triples dry up at high tier.

motivations.system: Pool copies and five of six tribes
motivations.player_wants: Take an uncontested tribe that is in the lobby.
motivations.tension: Contested tribes starve triples. One tribe is missing from each lobby, so plans must adapt.

motivations.player_wants: Hold pairs and hunt the third copy (Figgy Duff, Mistress Russet and Cut-and-Come-Again help).
motivations.tension: Pairs in hand cost board tempo. The payoff is the game's biggest multiplier: winners hold 3.6 goldens, 8th place 1.05.

motivations.player_wants: Pay a lump for a chosen high-tier unit.
motivations.tension: It is Created, so it sells for 0. It competes with buying units.

motivations.player_wants: Spend leftover gold on stats (1-5 per gold) or on economy. Harvest Supper rewards committing to one tribe, up to +3/+3.
motivations.tension: The flat, low rate makes late gold worth little and grow only linearly (under 1 stat per gold in practice).

motivations.player_wants: Lean into the hero's system: few units (Bracken), skipping tiers (March Hare), interest (Farthing), borrowing (Hob), tier down (Jill), a bigger shop (Pipkin).
motivations.tension: Concentration and climbing heroes win (2.70 and 3.57). Economy heroes lose (5.12-5.53).

motivations.player_wants: Rounds 1-2: choose a unit, Rainy Day or A Leg Up.
motivations.tension: Rainy Day pays 3 for a loss against 1 for a win (+1 Spoils), and losses cost almost nothing early. That is a mild reward for losing.

motivations.player_wants: Play greedy early, because early losses are cheap.
motivations.tension: The late game decides. The bottom half dies in rounds 11-14 before seeing tier 6.

owner_questions.question: How big should a winning board be at the end, and when tier 6 arrives? Today: about 35 stats per unit at the end (242 a board), 20 per unit at round 12.
owner_questions.why: It sets every budget number: tier curve, spell rate, growth caps. Measuring real games takes a research project; you can name the target from experience.
owner_questions.default_answer: Late carries at 100/100 or more and winning boards around 800-1,500 total, about 4-6× today, reached through compounding engines rather than bigger printed bodies. Mid-game boards around 25-40 per unit.

owner_questions.question: Where should compounding live: in gold (interest, max-gold raises, income engines) or in stats and 'this game' counters, with gold kept near flat at 10?
owner_questions.why: Both are legal under our rules, and they make very different games. Today gold is flat and nothing compounds.
owner_questions.default_answer: Like Battlegrounds: gold near flat (a few cards that raise max gold by 1). Compounding goes into 'this game' counters, shop-side buffs and per-gold stat engines, with caps only where gold or refreshes could loop.

owner_questions.question: Can we drop the power budget's linear growth caps and small per-trigger sizes, and police only loops (gold back per gold, free refreshes, retriggers)?
owner_questions.why: These caps are why every pass-2 card grows by 1-8 stats a turn. They are the rule your note pushes against.
owner_questions.default_answer: Yes. Keep the loop guards (G1, G2, G5, G8, Created sells for 0). Remove the growth caps. Judge engines by the tier at which they take over a game, not by stats per turn.

owner_questions.question: What climb pace should the game have?
owner_questions.why: Bots now reach tier 6 at round 14, four turns behind Battlegrounds' curve, and half the lobby never sees it. The pace is set by bot scripts, so it needs a target.
owner_questions.default_answer: Battlegrounds' standard 2/4/6/8/10, with the last climb back at 11. Most surviving players at tier 6 by round 11, greedy players by round 9.

owner_questions.question: Should every tribe have a way to stack stats on one carry, or should wide, even boards stay the norm with one or two tall tribes?
owner_questions.why: The budget treats stats as interchangeable. The data (Bracken, Dozey) suggest stacking wins. This decides how to rework the tribes.
owner_questions.default_answer: Every tribe gets at least one carry payoff that grows from its own actions, and each tribe keeps one stat-holder (cleave, damage reduction or shields). One or two tribes stay wide by design and get a counter to big carries.

owner_questions.question: Is banking gold meant to be a real strategy, or is carry-over just 'nothing is wasted'?
owner_questions.why: Nobody banks in the data, and the interest hero is last. That decides whether to build payoffs or leave it as a convenience.
owner_questions.default_answer: Mostly 'nothing is wasted', plus a few lump buys (Last Orders, Hiring Fair, a big climb). No tribe or hero built around interest.

maps.summary:
The data is clean: 400 complete lobbies, 3,200 players, and the run is finished. The orchestrator's figures check out with small drift (round 10 is 107, round 20 is 220, 0 early wins gives 21% top 4).

How many losses: Health runs on the round base. A loss costs about 1-2 Health in rounds 1-3, 3-4 in rounds 4-7, 5-7 in rounds 8-10, then 9, 11, 13 and about 15 from round 14. Nobody goes out before round 9. Losing every round from round 1 puts you out in round 11. Winning rounds 1-6 and then losing every round puts you out in round 12 after 6 losses. From round 13, 3 losses kill a hero at full Health. Last Stand gives the last four one more. Winners lose 5 fights; heroes who go out lose 6.7 to 8.6.

Wins: fights between living players are exactly 50/50. Ghosts lose 93.5%, which is the only reason the pooled rate is 51.3%. Ties happen only in round 1.

Stat curve: it is linear, about 12 to 14 per round. Stats per gold spent fall, from 1.41 at round 5 to 1.05 at round 22. The spread inside a lobby stays flat: the biggest board is about 1.2 times the median at every round. About half of every final board is printed bodies. Owner's view: right that numbers are small and don't compound. Concentration can't be measured from these files. The two most common cards on winning boards give buffs only during combat, and the logs record no combat stats at all.

findings.claim: The orchestrator's figures hold, with small drift because the file was still partial when they were read.
findings.evidence: a1_pace.py on rounds.csv and players.csv. Medians of attack+health over living players, by round. Lobby ratios are median over lobbies of max/median and min/median.
findings.numbers: Median board: R5 42, R8 80, R10 107, R12 133, R14 155, R16 174, R20 220. Per unit: R8 11.7, R12 19.7, R16 26.8, R20 34.4. Winners' final boards: median 242. Biggest board / lobby median: 1.18-1.25 from R4 to R19; smallest: 0.79-0.81. 1st place: 14.1 wins, 5.02 losses, 0.45 ties over 19.6 rounds. 8th: 2.17 wins, 8.58 losses over 11.2. Wins in R1-6: 0 wins gives mean place 6.00 and 21% top 4; 5 wins gives 83%; 6 wins gives 88%.

findings.claim: How many losses you can take depends on when they come. Late losses are nearly all round base, so after round 12 three losses kill a hero at full Health.
findings.evidence: Damage-v05 arm B charges (200 lobbies, same rule) give survivors per loss by round. That rate is scaled by 1.23 to fit pass 2 places 5-8 (a2b_calib.py), then paths are run in a2_hp.py.
findings.numbers: Cost per loss: R1-3 1.2-1.7; R4-7 3.0-4.4; R8-10 5.2-7.4; R11 9.4; R12 11.3; R13 13.2; R14+ about 15. Lose every round: out in R11 after 11 losses. Win R1-6 then lose: out in R12 after 6. Win R1-9 then lose: out in R13 after 4. Win R1-12 then lose: out in R15 after 3. Alternate W/L: out in R14 after 7 (a 5th place). Win 2 of every 3: out in R18 after 6. Losing all of R1-6 leaves about 25 Health. Losses per game by place: 1st 5.0 (range 0-10); 2nd-4th 6.7-7.4; 5th-8th 7.2-8.6. First elimination: median R11, never before R9.

findings.claim: Late in the game, how badly you lose barely matters: survivors are a small share of the damage.
findings.evidence: Arm B: survivor damage as a share of each loss, by round (a2_hp.py section 1). Pass 2: base taken by place (a2b_calib.py).
findings.numbers: Survivor share of a loss: 43-55% in R4-7, 25-33% in R8-10, 11-16% from R12. Survivors per loss stay about 1.6-1.9 (arm B) and about 2.0-2.35 (pass 2 places 5-8). Places 5-8 take 24.5-32.7 of base out of about 45-47 total.

findings.claim: Last Stand is used by nearly every 2nd and 3rd place, so the last four effectively get one extra lethal loss.
findings.evidence: Arm B last_stand_sides by final place. Pass 2: places 2-3 took more base damage than 40, which only the save allows. 'Certain' means base alone reached 40 before the hero's last loss.
findings.numbers: Arm B used Last Stand: 2nd 95%, 3rd 88%, 4th 55%, 1st 26%. Pass 2 mean base taken: 2nd 49.8, 3rd 48.8, 4th 44.5. Certain users: at least 30% of 2nd places and 11% of winners.

findings.claim: Fights between living players are exactly 50/50. The pooled surplus is all ghost fights. Per-player win rates spread 1.5 times wider than coin flips.
findings.evidence: a3_wins.py. Live-vs-live = all results minus ghost results (ghost results are inferred from wins minus losses in rounds with an odd number alive). The null case is coin flips with each player's own fight count.
findings.numbers: Live vs live: 22,925 wins and 22,925 losses. Pooled: 51.34%. Per-player rate: mean 47.6%, median 46.7%, sd 20.3 points against 13.4 for coin flips. By place: 74%, 65%, 60%, 50%, 45%, 37%, 30%, 20%.

findings.claim: Ties are almost gone. Results run in streaks, mostly because board strength persists from round to round.
findings.evidence: a3_wins.py sections 4-5 and a8_cond.py. Runs test on each player's decided fights. Correlation of a player's stats / lobby median between rounds (a4_curve.py section 5).
findings.numbers: Ties: 45.7% of R1 fights (67% of players field no unit in R1), and 0 of 45,573 player-fights after R1. Win chance after a win: 60.3%; after a loss: 41.0%. Runs test z = -22.9. Correlation of relative size: R8 to R10 0.76, R10 to R12 0.80, R4 to R12 only 0.20. Longest loss streak: 1st 2.4, 8th 6.3.

findings.claim: Total stats predict fights only in part. The biggest board loses about a quarter of its fights, and below-median boards hit a flat floor near 36%.
findings.evidence: a3_wins.py sections 2-3. Win rate by stat rank in rounds with 8 alive, and by stats / lobby median for R4+.
findings.numbers: Rank 1 wins 76-79% (if stats decided, 100%). Rank 8 wins 32-37% (if stats decided, 0%). Win rate by size: 1.2x median 74%, 1.3x 84%, 1.5x+ 94%, 0.65-0.95x 35-39% (flat), at or below 0.65x 27%.

findings.claim: The owner is right about ghosts: they are near-byes. They lose far more often than a living board of the same size. The code gives them three handicaps, and the files cannot separate them.
findings.evidence: a3_wins.py section 6, with the ghost board taken from the eliminated player's last round. game_session.gd:765-767: the ghost has no hero effects. game_session.gd:684-695: the scout of the ghost is exact because its board never changes, while a living opponent's scout is its board from the previous fight. hero_rules.gd:53-58: Last Stand only covers losses to a hero. Early Spoils pays nothing for beating a ghost.
findings.numbers: 1,461 ghost fights (3.65 per lobby). Living player wins 93.5%. Ghost size: median 0.82 of the lobby median, and smaller than every living board in 43% of its fights. Ghost win rate: 7.0% at 0.8-0.9x median (a living board that size wins about 36%), 18.7% at or above the median, 1.5% below 0.8x. 817 ghost fights come with 3 alive: one player in the final three gets a near-bye each round. Arm B ghosts won 8.2%.

findings.claim: The stat curve is linear, not compounding, and later gold buys fewer stats than early gold.
findings.evidence: a4_curve.py: least-squares fits on median stats for R5-16, increments per round, same-player increments, and board stats / total gold spent so far.
findings.numbers: Everyone: -19.4 + 12.38*round, R² 0.99, max error 4.7. Exponential: R² 0.92, max error 29. Winners: -24.2 + 14.07*round. Winners R8-19: power law with exponent 1.07. Gain per round +10 to +16, highest in R7-11 (median same-player gain: +15 at R8, +14 at R10), falling to +6-10 from R14. Growth rate: 40% at R5, 16% at R10, 7% at R16. Stats per gold: 1.41 at R5, 1.23 at R8, 1.18 at R12, 1.08 at R16, 1.05 at R22.

findings.claim: The gap between boards in a lobby doesn't grow in relative terms. Winners are only slightly bigger than their lobby until the end.
findings.evidence: a1_pace.py section 3 and a4_curve.py section 5.
findings.numbers: Coefficient of variation 0.14-0.17 every round R4-R19. Max/min 1.5-1.6. Absolute gap: 17 at R5, 34 at R8, 71 at R16 (only because everything grows). motivations.tension: Concentrated or blowout boards earn no extra damage late, so the clock rewards consistency over margin.

motivations.tension: Early wins predict place even at equal board size (3.09 against 4.19). The early economy, not Health, carries the advantage.

motivations.player_wants: One free lethal loss for a risky late turn
motivations.tension: Nearly all 2nd and 3rd places use it. This softens the top-four fight and makes the 4th-to-5th cliff sharper.
