motivations.system: Scouting the next opponent's last fought board
motivations.player_wants: To place units against what the next opponent showed last
motivations.tension: Living opponents change after being seen and the ghost doesn't, so the information is uneven.

motivations.system: Linear stats per gold, with half of the board being printed bodies
motivations.player_wants: To tier up and triple into fresh high-tier goldens rather than invest in scaling engines
motivations.tension: Scaling tribes and engines can't outgrow simply buying bodies. This matches the owner's 'too low and not compounding' concern.

owner_questions.question: In a healthy Battlegrounds meta, roughly what is a board's total stats and its top unit's stats at turns 8, 11, 14 and the end? And what share of the board do the top two units hold?
owner_questions.why: Our curve is 80, 121, 155 and 242 at R8, R11, R14 and the end, with per-unit 12, 18, 23 and 36. We have no target to aim at, and extracting one from videos takes days.
owner_questions.default_answer: Late per-unit stats about 5 times ours, mid-game about 2 times, top two units holding 40% or more of board stats. Agents check this against 10 high-MMR games.

owner_questions.question: Should a unit of gold buy clearly more stats late than early, so stats compound? Or is a linear curve built on high-tier goldens fine?
owner_questions.why: Stats per gold spent fall from 1.41 at R5 to 1.05 at R22. Almost all later design depends on which shape we aim for.
owner_questions.default_answer: Compound: aim for a working engine's stats per gold to rise from about 1.3 at mid-game to 3 or more late.

owner_questions.question: Is a ghost that loses 93.5% of its fights acceptable, as in Battlegrounds? Or should it keep its owner's hero power and stop the living player from seeing it exactly?
owner_questions.why: Ghost fights are near-byes, and 817 of them come in the final three.
owner_questions.default_answer: Give the ghost its owner's hero power, keep the rest as in Battlegrounds, and measure again.

owner_questions.question: Should a crushing late win hurt more than a narrow one? Today survivors are 11-16% of a loss from round 12.
owner_questions.why: If margin doesn't matter, the concentration and blowout boards the owner describes earn nothing extra in Health.
owner_questions.default_answer: Keep the base clock, but from round 10 make each survivor deal 2 instead of 1, then re-check pace.

maps.summary:
Under our rules the owner's example holds exactly: 3×10/11 beats 5×10/10 every time, with one survivor, whatever the placement or targeting. The reason is general. A fight is a count of exchanges, not a sum of damage. Each side makes one attack per turn, whatever its unit count. Every exchange costs both units a hit, and a dying unit still deals its damage. So a unit lasts ceil(Health ÷ enemy Attack) exchanges, and it kills in each one if its Attack is at least the enemy's Health. At equal total stats with even splits, the board with fewer units wins or ties every time (ties go to Last Blow, decided by parity).

But 'concentration' is not always better. A carry with small units below the enemy's breakpoints loses to an even board. On the 12 real pass 2 R9 boards (plain stat lines), +1/+1 on all seven units does about as well as +7/+7 on one unit. Moving a board's stats into one carry gains only about 2 to 3 points on average. What decides fights is breakpoints. Our small integers put a breakpoint under one third of unit pairs for every single point. For example, the same 65 stats as 5/6s win 96.5%, but as 6/5s in the back row they win 64.7%. Dozey's low-roll dominance is reproduced just as well by an even spread with 6 Health.

That breakpoint effect, plus near-deterministic combat (59 of 66 plain R9 pairs fall outside 10–90%), is why fixed-board tests swing 22–68 points. Scaling stats ×4 cuts a +1/+1 swing from about 30 to about 9 points. The pass 2 slice has almost no effects that let a unit hold its stats, and its answers to a carry mostly aim 'across'.

findings.claim: The owner's example is exact under our rules: three 10/11 always beat five 10/10 and end with exactly one survivor, whatever the placement, targeting or attack order.
findings.evidence: The five-unit board attacks first (rulebook 9.2.1; src/core/combat/combat.gd:378-383). Exchanges are simultaneous (9.6.1). A 10/10 dies to any hit. A 10/11 survives one hit on 1 Health and kills in both of its exchanges. Board A has 6 exchanges of life, board B has 5. Model run: all 35 three-slot placements × 4 five-unit layouts × 200 fights gave one outcome only, {(A wins, 1 survivor)}. Trace (trace_owner.py): B F1 trades into A F1 (A F1 left on 1 Health), A F1 kills B F4 and dies, and so on. B's 5th attacker dies and A's F3 is left at 10/1. Hero damage = round base + 1 (10.1.4a).
findings.numbers: 5 600 fights, 1 distinct outcome; survivors = 1

findings.claim: For plain units, a fight is decided by counting exchanges. A uniform board lasts n×ceil(h ÷ enemy A) exchanges. Whichever side lasts longer wins, and an exact tie goes to Last Blow by parity. At equal total stats with even splits, fewer bigger units win or tie every time.
findings.evidence: Model bramble_combat.py (mirrors combat.gd _choose_attacker, combat_lanes.gd normal_targets, 9.9.2 Last Blow): 0 violations of the law in 3 000 random uniform matchups. Equal totals, S=840: the 2-unit board beats 3 to 7 units 100%, 3 beats 4 to 7 100%, and so on. A single unit ties in exchange count with n=2..7, so the parity of the final exchange decides: it wins vs 2, 4 and 6 and loses vs 3, 5 and 7. The same pattern holds at S=70 and S=160 (equal_totals.txt).
findings.numbers: n≥2: fewer units win 100% at equal totals; 1 unit flips by parity

findings.claim: 'One carry plus small units' is not concentration that works. Units whose Attack is below the enemy's Health and whose Health is at or below the enemy's Attack are worth one exchange each, whatever their stats. So a carry with chaff loses to an even board.
findings.evidence: carry.txt, all boards 84 stats vs 7×6/6: 12/12+6×5/5 wins 0%, 24/24+6×3/3 wins 15.4% (F1) or 8.1% (B2), 36/36+6×1/1 wins 6.2%. 42/42 alone wins 0% (a tie in exchange count, lost on parity). A 26/26+2×8/8 board wins 100%. A carry c/c+6×8/8 vs 7×9/9 (126 stats) needs c=38 (172 stats) to reach 63%.
findings.numbers: carry+chaff 0-15% at equal stats; needs about 1.37× the stats when the chaff sits one point below the enemy's breakpoints

findings.claim: On realistic boards (the 12 pass 2 R9 boards as plain stat lines), concentration gives small average gains with large per-board swings. A buff spread over all units does as well as the same buff on one unit, or slightly better.
findings.evidence: realloc.txt (each board keeps its total, slots and attack share), win % vs the 11 originals: even 50.7, 25% carry in front 52.5, 40% front 52.5, 40% back 47.5, 55% front 53.3. Per board it ranges from hunters_low same-roll 65.6→85.6 to hedgerow_low 97.2→68.8. r9_conc.txt: +1/+1 all 68.9 vs +7/+7 on the biggest 68.1 vs on the smallest 71.1; +2/+2 all 84.9 vs +14/+14 biggest 80.6.
findings.numbers: carry premium about +2 to +3 pp on average; spread ≥ concentrated for 14 to 28 stats of buff

findings.claim: Breakpoints, not concentration as such, dominate. Win rate is a step function of stats relative to the opponent's. Dozey's low-roll dominance is reproduced by an even spread whose units all have 6 Health.
findings.evidence: breakpoints.txt, 7×A/H vs 7×10/10: 0% when A≤9 and H≤10; about 50% when exactly one of A≥10 or H≥11 holds; 100% when both hold, or when H≥21 even with A=7. Results are flat between the steps. dozey.txt vs the 5 other low boards (1 000 fights each): Dozey 10/16 board 95.7%; six 5/6s (65 stats) 96.5%; same totals as 5/6 front and 6/5 back 64.7%. bp_share.txt at R9 scale: +1 Attack cuts the hits needed against 32.7% of enemy units, and +1 Health adds a survived hit against 26.3%.
findings.numbers: one Health point (6 vs 5) swings about 32 pp; R9 unit median 4/6

findings.claim: Plain stat lines alone explain most of the real R9 matrix. The extremes and the +1/+1 sensitivity come mainly from the combat rules, not from card text.
findings.evidence: r9_plain_vs_real.txt: Pearson r 0.81 over 132 ordered pairs. Plain and real pick the same favourite in 114 of 132. Plain hedgerow_low same-roll 96.5% vs real 99.6%. Plain +1/+1 sensitivity +1.3 to +69.1 pp (mean 30) vs the real +0.4 to +68.1 (docs/ideation/evidence/pass2-followup/r9-results.md). The biggest gaps where text matters: hedgerow_high vs bog_high (plain 0%, real 88%) and oozes_high vs hunters_high (3% vs 76%).
findings.numbers: r=0.81; 114/132 same favourite

findings.claim: Fixed-board tests are this sensitive for five reasons. Combat is near-deterministic. Integers are small. +1/+1 on a whole board is a 16–27% buff applied in one direction to every unit. The opponent never varies. Exact ties are settled by parity.
findings.evidence: exp_lastblow.py: 59 of 66 plain R9 pairs fall outside 10–90%, and 5.0% of fights end in a Last Blow mutual wipe. The only randomness left is the front-row target pick, the first-attacker coin when unit counts are equal, and Start of Combat order. R9 boards hold 52–114 stats, so +14 is 12–27%. In the lobby, +20% stats ≈ +24 pp (1.0× median 51.9% → 1.2× 75.9%, lobby_stats.txt). scale.txt (stats ×k with jitter): +1/+1 swing 30.3 → 16.6 → 9.1 → 3.4 pp at k=1, 2, 4, 10, while +10% stays 15–19 pp.
findings.numbers: +1/+1 swing falls about 1/k with stat scale; +10% stays about 15 pp

findings.claim: Which rules strengthen concentration and which weaken it.
findings.evidence: Strengthen: one attack per side per turn (9.4.1), so a lone carry attacks every turn. Simultaneous return damage, with the dying unit still dealing its damage (9.6.1/9.6.3), so Health counts in whole multiples of enemy Attack. Random front-row targeting (9.5.5), so a carry is focused only by text (Mire, Snap, Quarry). Back-row protection (9.5.1): Dozey in B3 96.4% vs F4 90.0% vs F1 83.9% against low boards. Flat combat effects (Bitter, Hex, Jack Daw, -1/-1, 2–3 damage) take a bigger share of small units. Brother Bracken (+X/+X with 5 or fewer units) is the top hero, mean place 2.70 vs next best 3.57 (players.csv). Weaken: no trample, so overkill is lost and every body absorbs a whole exchange. Hero damage counts surviving starting units (10.1.4a): the owner's example leaves 1, and plain R9 wins leave 2.15 on average. More units attack first and win odd-length exact ties (9.2.1, 9.9.2). Permanent-buff ceilings (Dozey +12/+12, Bridge Toad +3/+3; 12.1.1a), the Ring cap +4/+4 (8.5.4) and the Supper cap +3/+3 (5.2.9). No cleave or windfury in the slice.

findings.claim: In pass 2 almost nothing lets a unit hold its stats while killing. There is no Divine Shield, Reborn, Cleave, Windfury, Venomous or damage reduction.
findings.evidence: Grep of content/units/*.json with set 'slice' (units.txt). What exists: Pack joiners deal damage but take no return hit (combat.gd _strikes: hits_back go only to the leader): Wick, Brother Wolf, Grey Agnes, Grizel, Old Isegrim (+3 Attack while joining). Barn Owl takes no damage while attacking the back row (mechanics/back_row_immunity.gd). Bitter shrinks the attacker before damage on pass 2: Warty Nan, Peatling, Madame Bufo, Natterjack Chorus, Prima Donna, Peat King's Peatlings. Attack shrinkers across: Hex, Jenny -2, Toll Bard, Jack Daw, Seven Whistlers. Turnip Scarecrow makes the enemy across skip an attack, but the turn passes to its next unit. Extra bodies: Bellies, Bubble and Squeak, Wee Wobbly, Earwig Mother, Mrs Sorrel, Peat King, Will-o'-the-Wisp, Mousewife, Gabble Ratchet. Model, giving Dozey one keyword (vs all 11 plain boards, base 46.7%): takes 2 less damage +24.5, immune while attacking +20.5, Hunker +15.1, Bitter 2 +13.8, shield +13.3, cleave +11.0, windfury +4.4.
findings.numbers: damage reduction or immunity is the strongest carry amplifier in our rules (+20 to +25 pp)

findings.claim: Answers to one big unit ('scam' units) do exist in pass 2, but nearly all are aimed at 'the enemy across'. They hit a carry only when the two layouts line up. There is no poison, no 'destroy the biggest' and no 'set Health'.
findings.evidence: Answers that ignore size or work in percentages: Belladonna's Nightshade (loses half its current Health each time it is attacked; combat_moves.gd nightshade), Hasty Pudding (swallows the enemy across), Changeling (borrows the enemy across for one attack), Ichneumon Wasp (an enemy it damages dies after its next attack; parasite.gd), Madame Bufo (her killer loses half its Attack). Focus fire: Snap (attacks the Mired enemy with the most Attack), Mire forcing, Gideon and Jenny counter-attacks, Lantern Man. Reach into the back row: Barn Owl, Ballooning Spider, Old Lutra and Old Brock quarry 'wherever it stands', Whirligig row swap, Belladonna from the back. Hero: Little King Wren borrows the highest enemy Attack. Model: Nightshade on Dozey −28.5 pp; one venom front unit on every opponent −12.2; Bitter 2 on every enemy front unit −28.2 (Bitter repeats on every attack).
findings.numbers: Nightshade −28.5 pp; venom −12.2 pp

findings.claim: Bot lobby stat scale is about 5–6× below the owner's Battlegrounds picture, and lobby fights are strongly decided by relative stats. Bracken's 5-unit boards win about what their combat-time totals predict: a little more when ahead, a lot less when behind.
findings.evidence: free_choice_plain.rounds.csv (400 seeds, 3 200 players, complete; the .0. files named in the brief no longer exist). Median board total: round 9 92 (13.5 per unit), round 15 162 (25.0), round 20 220 (34.4). First place's final board 110/128 on 7 units. Win % by board total ÷ lobby-round median: 0.9–1.0× 41.0, 1.0–1.1× 53.3, 1.2–1.3× 75.4, 1.4–1.5× 91.0. Bracken 5-unit boards (rounds 7+, adding +min(tier,5)/+min(tier,5) per unit): 1.2× 83.5% vs 75.9% for 7-unit boards; 0.9× 25.6% vs 35.4%.
findings.numbers: late unit about 16/18 vs about 100/100 in BG; Bracken boards +3 to +8 pp when ahead, −10 pp when behind

findings.claim: Plain combat doesn't depend on scale except for granularity, so 'our numbers are too small' is half right. Bigger numbers would make tuning steps finer and flat effects smaller. They would not change a unit's power relative to its peers, which is where Dozey's strength comes from. His doubling is capped at +8/+8, so a bigger general scale would shrink him relative to his peers; an uncapped doubling would keep its power at any scale.
findings.evidence: Multiplying every stat by k leaves the exchange counts unchanged except for rounding (scale.txt: +10% stays about 15 pp at every k). Dozey's R9 line is 10/16 vs a board median of 4/6 (bp_share.txt), and that size ratio is what kills 3 to 4 units. Card text: content/units/alderman_dozey.json, 'double its stats, up to +8/+8', permanent_buff_cap 12.

findings.claim: The main checkout and pass 2 run different combat code for Bitter and Mire.
findings.evidence: ideation/main applies Bitter after the damage exchange (src/core/combat/combat_reactions.gd:113; the comment at 104-105 says it 'doesn't alter the same attack's damage'). The keyword text says 'first loses', and pass 2 applies it at declaration (Bramble-ideation-balance src/core/combat/combat_reactions.gd:55). Mire's 'waits for it, once' exists only on pass 2 (combat_lanes.gd:156 wait_once). My model follows pass 2.

assumptions.assumption: One stat point (SP) is 1 Attack or 1 Health. Points add up across a card and a board and are priced linearly.
assumptions.evidence_for: Removing one unit from a full board costs 21–23 pp (power-budget §6.4): each body ≈ one exchange. For marginal buffs on full R9 boards, +1/+1 on all ≈ +7/+7 on one (68.9 vs 68.1%).
assumptions.evidence_against: A point's value is a step function of the opponent's breakpoints: at equal totals, 5/6s win 96.5% and 6/5s in the back win 64.7%. Fewer bigger units beat more units at equal totals 100% (n≥2). Carry plus chaff loses at equal totals.
assumptions.test: Price cards by win-rate gain against a sample of real same-round lobby boards, not by SP sums, and report the size ratio to typical units.

assumptions.assumption: The tier curve is linear (V(t) ≈ 1.8t+3, tier 6 = 14 SP) with ±15% tolerance.
assumptions.evidence_for: Fits printed Battlegrounds medians (R² about 0.5).
assumptions.evidence_against: In exchange combat a unit 2× its peers both one-shots them and survives their hits, so it kills 2–4 of them (Dozey 10/16 vs a median 4/6). The fight value of size is superlinear near breakpoints. At small stats, ±15% is under one point, and one point crosses a breakpoint against 26–33% of enemy units.
assumptions.test: Measure win % vs the size ratio (unit stats ÷ lobby median) per round from lobby snapshots. Check whether the tier steps produce the ratios we want.

assumptions.assumption: Fixed-board round robins (R9) and their +1/+1 sensitivity measure board and card strength smoothly enough to tune with.
assumptions.evidence_for: Plain stats reproduce the real matrix (r=0.81), so the tests are internally consistent.
assumptions.evidence_against: 59 of 66 plain pairs fall outside 10–90%, and +1/+1 moves results 1–69 pp. The swing is set by where breakpoints fall, not by smooth strength.
assumptions.test: Report results against 50+ boards sampled from the same round of real lobbies, and curves over +k stats, instead of single fixed pairs.

assumptions.assumption: Stats are big enough that +1 is a fine tuning step.
assumptions.where: implicit in costing and balance passes (±1 SP steps)
assumptions.evidence_for: Late units reach about 16/18, so +1 is about 6% there.
assumptions.evidence_against: At R9 (where most tests run) the unit median is 4/6, and one point is 15–25% of a stat. The +1/+1 swing falls from 30 to 9 pp when stats are ×4.
assumptions.test: Rerun the R9 sensitivity with all stats ×3–4. Check whether tier 1–3 can carry finer steps.

assumptions.assumption: Caps (Dozey +12/+12, Bridge Toad +3/+3, Ring +4/+4, Supper +3/+3) are the right brake on outliers.
assumptions.evidence_for: Caps stop runaway loops, and Dozey's board dominated the low roll.
assumptions.evidence_against: The owner reads Hedgerow's overperformance as a sign that the other tribes are too small. An even spread with 6 Health does as well as Dozey, so the fault is breakpoints in a low-stat field, not size alone.
assumptions.test: Raise the scale of every tribe instead of capping one, then rerun the lobby benchmark and compare spread in tribe placements.

assumptions.assumption: Answers aimed at 'the enemy across' are fair answers to a carry.
assumptions.where: pass 2 content: Pudding, Changeling, Belladonna, Mire, Hex, Jack Daw, Quarry and others
assumptions.evidence_for: They create placement play on fixed slots.
assumptions.evidence_against: They hit the carry only when the two layouts line up, and the carry's owner controls where it stands. There are no size-based targeting answers in the slice besides Snap (which needs Mire).
assumptions.test: Log how often across-answers land on the opponent's highest-stat unit in bot lobbies.

assumptions.assumption: Last Blow (mutual wipe goes to the final attacker) and 'more units attacks first' are harmless tie rules.
assumptions.evidence_for: Only 5.0% of plain R9 fights end that way, and the rule removes ties after round 1 (0 ties in rounds 2+).
assumptions.evidence_against: It turns exact exchange ties into 0% or 100% by parity: a lone 42/42 loses to 7×6/6 at equal stats because 7 is odd.
assumptions.test: Count Last Blow endings in the real engine's lobby logs per round.

assumptions.assumption: The row values and placement rules in power-budget §6 (back-row Attack 0.75 SP and so on) carry over.
assumptions.evidence_for: Measured in a toy simulation.
assumptions.evidence_against: They were measured on small vanilla Tier 2 and Tier 5 boards, so they bake in that scale's breakpoints. Carry placement depends on the board: B3 was best for Dozey, while a 40% carry in the back did worse than in front on average (47.5 vs 52.5%).
assumptions.test: Re-measure the row coefficients after any change of stat scale.

assumptions.assumption: My plain Python model is a fair stand-in for the engine's rules without text.
assumptions.evidence_for: It reproduces the lives law exactly, the attack order of the 9.4 example (F1, F3, B2 repeat), and r=0.81 against the real R9 matrix.
assumptions.evidence_against: It ignores text, Bellies and Start of Combat effects, and it uses pass 2 Bitter timing. Rings and Eggs were added by hand from the board notes.
assumptions.test: Run the same plain boards through Godot once the machine is free and compare.

assumptions.assumption: rounds.csv attack and health are recruit-board stats taken before Start of Combat.
assumptions.evidence_for: Bracken's 5-unit boards sit at 0.86× the median before the adjustment, which fits a hero that trades bodies for a combat buff.
assumptions.evidence_against: Not checked against the writer code.
assumptions.test: Check the bench writer for when the stats are captured.

motivations.system: Exchange combat (9.4–9.6): one attack per side per turn, simultaneous return damage
motivations.player_wants: Every unit above the lobby's breakpoints: Attack at least the typical enemy Health (one-shot), and Health above the typical enemy Attack (survive one hit). Health counts in multiples of enemy Attack; Attack counts in fractions of enemy Health.
motivations.tension: Points between breakpoints are wasted, and the breakpoints move with the opponent, so the right build is a guess about the field.

motivations.system: Board size and who attacks first (9.2.1), each body ≈ one exchange
motivations.player_wants: Fill all 7 slots: each body absorbs at least one exchange, and the bigger board attacks first and wins odd-length exact ties.
motivations.tension: At a fixed stat total, fewer bigger units win. Brother Bracken pays players to stop at 5, and he is the best hero (mean place 2.70).

motivations.player_wants: Hitters in front. A carry or 'while alive' unit behind a front row that trades evenly, so the carry meets a thinned enemy board.
motivations.tension: Back units attack later and fight fewer exchanges. A carry behind a weak front does worse than in front (47.5 vs 52.5% on average).

motivations.system: Effects aimed 'across' (Mire, Quarry, Hex, Pudding, Changeling, Belladonna, Jack Daw, Scarecrow)
motivations.player_wants: Their own answers across the opponent's carry, and their own carry across an empty or weak enemy slot.
motivations.tension: Without the opponent's layout this is a guessing game, so answers land on carries by chance.

motivations.system: Hero damage = round base + surviving starting units (10.1.4a)
motivations.player_wants: Win with many units alive, which favours wide boards.
motivations.tension: Concentrated wins leave few survivors (1 in the owner's example, 2.15 on average in plain R9 wins), so a strategy that wins more fights deals less per win.

motivations.system: Flat combat effects and caps (Bitter, Hex, -2 Attack, 2–3 damage; +4/+4 Rings, +3/+3 Supper, +12/+12 Dozey)
motivations.player_wants: Units big enough that flat effects stop mattering, and spreading buffs across slots and tribes where caps block piling.
motivations.tension: Caps limit concentration while flat effects reward it, so the system pushes both ways at once.

owner_questions.question: When you say concentrating stats is always better, do you mean (a) at a fixed stat total, fewer bigger bodies win, or (b) a buff on one unit beats the same buff spread across the board?
owner_questions.why: Our rules make (a) true every time (n≥2). (b) is roughly a tie on real R9 boards (+1/+1 on all 68.9% vs +7/+7 on one 68.1%). The two readings lead to different design work.
owner_questions.default_answer: (a). Build carry tools and answers on that reading, and keep spread buffs priced as they are.

owner_questions.question: In a healthy Battlegrounds late game, roughly what share of a board's stats sits in its top two units, and how big is the top unit compared with the board average?
owner_questions.why: This gives the power budget a concentration target to aim at. You can answer it faster than video research can measure it.
owner_questions.default_answer: The top two units hold about 40% of the board's stats, and the top unit is about 2× the board average.

owner_questions.question: Should we raise the number scale about 3–5× (bodies, buffs, growth), and make flat combat effects (Bitter, Hex, 2–3 damage, -1/-1) scale with tier or work as percentages?
owner_questions.why: A +1/+1 swing on fixed boards falls from about 30 pp to about 9 pp at ×4, while +10% stays about 15 pp. Flat effects shrink with scale. Relative power, Dozey's included, does not change with scale.
owner_questions.default_answer: Yes, about ×4 by the late game, keeping tier 1 small. Convert flat combat effects to tier-scaled amounts.

owner_questions.question: Do you want deliberate 'hold stats while killing' keywords (a shield, damage reduction, a cleave) in the vanilla game, paired with answers based on size (percentage Health loss, 'attacks the highest-Health enemy', poison-like)?
owner_questions.why: The slice has almost none of the first. Its answers mostly aim 'across', so they land on a carry by chance. In the model, damage reduction adds +24.5 pp to a carry board and Nightshade takes away 28.5.
owner_questions.default_answer: Yes. Add two holding keywords and two size-based answers, spread across tribes, and cost them against real lobby boards.

maps.summary:
I audited all 48 pool cards in Birds, Bog folk and Fairies (16 each) against the card JSON, the engine code and the ideation rules. The full per-card table is in the detail file.

The main result: none of the three tribes has a permanent pile of stats that the player picks, protects and grows from gold. Hedgerow has one.
- **Birds** have one uncapped grower, the Cuckoo. But the Bird it grows is away, so it fights as an Egg at half stats unless Redwing stands beside it. Redwing and the Cuckoo compete for the same slot next to the Nest.
- **Bog**'s permanent growth is small and rate-limited: Ranocchio +1/+1 a fight, Tiddy Mun +2/+2 a fight, Bridge Toad capped at +3/+3. Nine of its 13 stat payoffs last one fight only.
- **Fairies** keep their power on slots, capped at +4/+4 a slot. Only the Queen concentrates, and only on a board with a single other Fairy.

What sets Hedgerow apart: Acorns are gold that turns straight into stats, Pass lets the player choose the carry, and its late payoffs only need a full board.

The owner's claim checks out for Birds (worst in every measure), partly for Bog, and is not shown for Fairies: their high-roll test board wins 77% (best of the high rolls), and bots picked Fairies only 29 times in 3,200 seats.

The bot data shows almost no snowballing (best board under 2x the median). Average units at round 16 are about 13/14, and highroll piles reach 25-30 per stat: 4-8x below the owner's Battlegrounds reference. Bufo, Belladonna and Changeling shrink big units proportionally, so they gain value if stats rise. The flat debuffs (Bitter, Jenny's -2 Attack, Jack Daw, Hex) lose value.

findings.claim: Each tribe's biggest-unit route is blocked by structure, not by numbers. Birds: one uncapped grower (Cuckoo), but its Bird is away and shows at half stats. Bog: no permanent pile beyond Ranocchio's +1/+1 a fight. Fairies: Rings capped at +4/+4 a slot; only the Queen concentrates, and she needs a board with one other Fairy.
findings.evidence: Card files content/units/{cuckoo,redwing,signor_ranocchio,tiddy_mun,bridge_toad,queen_of_elfland}.json. Rule 12.1.4: Eggs fight at half stats (docs/design/rulebook.md:790). Rule 8.5.4: the Ring cap (rulebook.md:506). Engine: src/core/mechanics/teind.gd splits the Queen's pool evenly among every other Fairy; board_geometry.gd:15 makes 'adjacent' the same row only, so 'beside' reaches at most 2 units.
findings.numbers: Concentrating stat payoffs, yes / partly: Birds 4/3 of 11, Bog 1/3 of 13 (the 1 is Lantern Man, combat only), Fairies 1/3 of 16, Hedgerow 6 of 13. Biggest unit as a multiple of the average unit on a highroll: Birds about 1.5-2x, Bog about 1.2x permanent (1.8x for Lantern Man's combat Attack), Fairies about 1.1-1.3x unless the Queen is fed into one Fairy.

findings.claim: Most payoffs in these tribes last one fight only, and Bog's almost entirely so. Permanent growth is slow and capped early: Bridge Toad stops at 4/6 by about round 5, Peat Cutter pays 3 gold in all, Rings stop at +4/+4 by rounds 8-10, Hex stops at your tier. Every Bog grower is limited to once or twice a fight.
findings.evidence: permanent_buff_cap 3 (bridge_toad.json:37). Limits: signor_ranocchio.json:20 (once), tiddy_mun.json:18 and peat_king.json:21 (twice). Peat Cutter's 'lifetime': 3. Hex 'most': 'tier'. Rule 12.1.1a (rulebook.md:780) caps feeding, Pinches and permanent combat gains.
findings.numbers: Combat-only stat payoffs: Bog 9 of 13, Birds 6 of 11 (plus Mother Goose's strikes), Fairies 6 of 16, Hedgerow 4 of 13. Bog's best permanent growth on a highroll is about +6 stats a fight (Ranocchio 2 + Tiddy 4). The Cuckoo gives about +6 a turn. Annis, Hob, Lob and Sally give +2 a turn each.

findings.claim: Only Hedgerow can turn spare gold into stats inside the tribe and keep compounding. Birds' route is slow (Mrs Stork brings Mother Goose home, at most every 2 turns), Bog has no route at all, and Fairies' route is the Queen.
findings.evidence: Hedgerow: alderman_dozey.json ('Feeding rounds up', so 1 Acorn = +1/+1), mr_pym (Pass +2/+2 per Stash), beadle_warrenby, goodman_hayward, old_mother_mast. Birds: one_swallow and mrs_jay pay 1 gold or 1 Acorn a cycle, and flights pay no sale gold (12.1.4). Bog: young_pretender and peat_cutter pay gold that no Bog card spends.
findings.numbers: Stork + Goose: about 14 stats, spread, per 6 gold. Queen: about 30 stats per 3 turns for 6 gold of rebuys (golden: about 60). Hedgerow: 2 stats per gold onto Dozey, plus +1/+1 on every touching Hedgerow unit per Stash with Hayward.

findings.claim: Hedgerow's edge is structural: its economy and stats share one currency (Acorns), the player chooses and protects the carry (Pass, Dozey), its late payoffs need only a full board, and its growth is permanent. The evidence splits on which of these matters. Bot wins track the board-wide Start of Combat buffs and the Acorn economy; the constructed test boards track concentration in Dozey.
findings.evidence: Bot final boards (free_choice_plain.cards.csv joined to players.csv, scratch scripts/bots4.py). Constructed round-9 boards: docs/ideation/evidence/pass2-followup/r9-results.md and pass2-followup-boards.md.
findings.numbers: Bot Hedgerow boards with Squire Lollop: mean place 2.18, 47.9% first (n=146). With Standing Committee: 2.89, 36.2%. With Old Mother Mast: 2.62. With Alderman Dozey: 4.07, worse than without him (3.58). Constructed low roll: hedgerow_low wins 99.6% with Dozey at 10/16, 40% of its 65 stats.

findings.claim: The owner's hypothesis ('Hedgerow is fine; others are too weak') is right for Birds, partly right for Bog, and not shown for Fairies.
findings.evidence: build/sim/pass2-followup/lobbies/free_choice_plain.summary.csv (400 lobbies, 3,200 seats). Constructed round-9 same-roll results: r9-results.md.
findings.numbers: Birds: mean place 5.10 (CI 4.91-5.29), 4.9% first, high board 34.5%. Bog: 4.30, 12.8% first (fair share is 12.5%), high 28.3%, low 61.9%. Fairies: high board 77.0% (best of the highs), low 10.2%; only 29 bot seats. Hedgerow: 3.75, 25.3% first, high 44.9%, low 99.6%.

findings.claim: Concentration helps once the big unit clears the enemy's Attack and Health thresholds. Below them, the total still matters. And stats parked in textless Eggs underperform.
findings.evidence: Scratch scripts/fixtures2.py over the constructed round-9 boards.
findings.numbers: hedgerow_low: 65 total, biggest 10/16, wins 99.6%. fairies_low: 50 total, biggest 8/10 (36% of its stats), wins 10.2%. birds_high: 102 total, the most of any board, with two 9/10-ish Eggs, wins 34.5%. Caveat: +1/+1 on every unit moves most boards by 30-68 percentage points, so these are threshold tests.

findings.claim: Bot play shows almost no snowballing and a low stat scale. It cannot measure the curve shape the owner cares about.
findings.evidence: free_choice_plain.rounds.csv (all seats), scratch scripts/bots3.py.
findings.numbers: Board stat totals: round 8 median 80, top 1% 116, max 129. Round 12: 133 / 191 / 226. Round 16: 174 / 266 / 318 (top 1% is 1.53x the median). The biggest board in a lobby is 1.22x the lobby median at round 12 (1.38 at the 90th percentile). Gold at the start of round 12: median 12, top 1% 17. Average stats per unit at round 16: 26-30, about 13/14.

findings.claim: Typical and highroll estimates, combat stats (stats per unit and biggest unit). Birds: 11 and 6/8 typical, 14 and 9/10 highroll at round 8; 18 and 11/12 typical, 21 and 18/19 highroll at round 12; 25 and 19/20 typical, 29 and 25/26 to 30/31 highroll at round 16. Bog: 11 and 4/6-3/7 typical, 12 and 8/9 highroll at round 8; 19 and 8/9 typical, 20 and 12/13 highroll at round 12 (Lantern Man 22/11 in combat); 26 and 13/14 typical, 27 and 16/17 to 21/25 highroll at round 16 (Lantern Man 25/11, golden 47/19). Fairies: 10 and 6/8 typical, 13 and 8/11 highroll at round 8; 17 and 9/12 typical, 23 and 12/20 highroll at round 12; 23 and 12/16 typical, 28 and 12/21 highroll at round 16. A Queen-fed lone Fairy reaches about 44/68 at round 16.
findings.evidence: Growth arithmetic in scratch scripts/growth.py. Highroll round-8 values match the constructed round-9 boards (pass2-followup-boards.md). Typical averages match bot recruit stats.
findings.numbers: Bot recruit stats per unit at rounds 8/12/16: Birds 12.0/19.6/26.5, Bog 12.3/20.4/27.4, Fairies 12.2/19.8/29.3 (n=29/26/15), Hedgerow 12.1/20.7/27.0.

findings.claim: The two Bird routes work against each other, and the Cuckoo does not pay off in bot hands.
findings.evidence: Old Tern, Mrs Stork and Mrs Dunnock bring Birds home early, which cuts the trips the Cuckoo lengthens (held_units.gd land_flock and shorten_trip). Redwing and the Cuckoo both need the same-row slot next to the Nest (board_geometry.gd:15).
findings.numbers: Bot Bird boards: with the Cuckoo, mean place 5.61 vs 4.57 without; with Mrs Stork, 5.44 vs 4.75. Only 66 of 371 Bird boards had the Cuckoo together with Redwing, the Great Lump or the Gabble Ratchet.

findings.claim: The answers to big units divide by type. The ones that shrink a unit by a share grow stronger as stats rise: Madame Bufo halves Attack, Belladonna's Nightshade halves current Health each time the unit is attacked, and the Changeling turns the enemy's carry on its own team. The flat ones weaken: Bitter, Jenny's -2 Attack, Jack Daw's 2-Attack steal, Hex capped at your tier.
findings.evidence: combat_moves.gd:248-257 (Nightshade); madame_bufo.json, changeling.json, jack_daw.json, hedge_witch.json, jenny_greenteeth.json.
findings.numbers: Against a 30/30 carry: Nightshade takes 15 Health before the first hit, Bufo leaves it at 14 Attack, and the Changeling deals 30 to its own side. Jack Daw takes 2 (7%). Bitter 2 takes about 7%.

findings.claim: The bot lobby data has measurement gaps that bias it against Birds, Fairies and Bog, and the files have changed since the brief.
findings.evidence: tools/sim/bench.gd:383-393 sums combat_spec (base + permanent + tribe bonus; recruit_unit.gd:180-189), so auras, Rings, Eggs and combat-only effects are left out. The benchmark is complete: progress.json shows stage 'complete'. The files are free_choice_plain.*.csv; the hidden .0 files named in the brief don't exist.
findings.numbers: 400 lobbies, 3,200 seats, no missing fields. Fairies were chosen in 29 of 2,576 seats where they were in the lobby. Queen of Elfland is on 653 final boards, 634 of them not Fairy boards, where Teind only destroys.

findings.claim: The design docs and the shipped cards have drifted apart; the JSON is what the game plays.
findings.evidence: pass2-b.md gives Ranocchio 3/5, twice a fight; the JSON has 3/4, once a fight. pass2-bog.md gives Tiddy Mun 'first, +2 Health' and Bridge Toad 'once a fight'; the JSON has Tiddy +1/+1 after the hit, twice a fight, and the Toad capped 'up to +3/+3'. src/core/mechanics/bitter.gd still says Bitter applies after damage, while combat_reactions.gd:55 applies it at declaration, as rule 9.6.0 says.

assumptions.assumption: Eggs fighting at half stats is a fair price for flying.
assumptions.evidence_for: The designers wanted flying to cost tempo (docs/ideation/content/birds.md).
assumptions.evidence_against: Birds are last in lobbies (place 5.10, 4.9% first). birds_high has the biggest round-9 total (102) and wins 34.5%. Bot boards with the Cuckoo place worse.
assumptions.test: Constructed round-12 and round-16 Bird boards with Eggs at half vs full Health, against the other tribes' boards at the same rounds.

assumptions.assumption: The Ring cap of +4/+4 a slot keeps Fairies fair without flattening them.
assumptions.evidence_for: fairies_high wins 77% at round 9.
assumptions.evidence_against: The only Fairy concentrator is the Queen, and she works against Fairy Monarch and Harvest Supper. fairies_low wins 10.2%. The biggest standing Fairy at round 16 is about 12/21.
assumptions.test: Round-12 and round-16 Fairy test boards with the cap at 4, at 8, and scaled with tier.

assumptions.assumption: Once- and twice-a-fight limits keep Bog's growth safe without making it irrelevant.
assumptions.evidence_for: pass2-bog.md section 8 worried that late walls would grind fights out slowly.
assumptions.evidence_against: Bog's best permanent growth is about +6 stats a fight. The owner wants bigger numbers, and wants rewards to give power.
assumptions.test: Round-12 and round-16 Bog test boards with Ranocchio at twice a fight and Tiddy Mun at three times.

assumptions.assumption: Flat answers (Bitter 1-2, Jenny's -2 Attack, Jack Daw's 2, Hex up to your tier) stay relevant at any stat scale.
assumptions.evidence_for: They are fine at round-9 scale, where enemy Attack is 5-8.
assumptions.evidence_against: Their value falls in proportion as stats rise. The proportional answers (Bufo, Belladonna, Changeling) gain.
assumptions.test: Re-run the round-9 test boards with every stat doubled.

assumptions.assumption: Bot board totals compare tribes fairly.
assumptions.evidence_for: The same measure is used for every tribe.
assumptions.evidence_against: The totals leave out auras, Rings, Eggs and combat-only power, so they understate Birds, Fairies and Bog.
assumptions.test: Log each unit's stats at the start of combat in the bench.

assumptions.assumption: Bot lobbies can rate Fairies.
assumptions.evidence_against: Only 29 Fairy seats. Bots play Queen of Elfland on 634 non-Fairy boards, where her Teind only destroys their own units.
assumptions.test: Use the constructed boards for Fairies; ignore the lobby rate.

assumptions.assumption: Birds' two routes (Homecoming and Hatchery) can mix.
assumptions.evidence_for: Mother Goose and the Cuckoo serve both routes.
assumptions.evidence_against: Old Tern, Mrs Stork and Mrs Dunnock end Cuckoo trips early, and Redwing competes with the Cuckoo for the slot beside the Nest.
assumptions.test: Round-12 test boards: Hatchery only vs a mixed board.

assumptions.assumption: Bog walls survive long enough for its on-attacked payoffs to fire.
assumptions.evidence_for: Making Bitter hit first moved Bog's high board from 12% to 51% (pass2-bog.md section 6).
assumptions.evidence_against: On a board one Supper short, Bog falls to 3.5%: a cliff.
assumptions.test: Sweep enemy Attack against the Bog test boards.

assumptions.assumption: Hedgerow's lead comes from its structure, not from two cards.
assumptions.evidence_for: Its Acorn economy feeds its stats directly, and the Dozey low-roll board wins 99.6%.
assumptions.evidence_against: Its lobby wins track Squire Lollop and Standing Committee (47.9% and 36.2% first when on the final board); Dozey boards do worse.
assumptions.test: Replace Lollop and Committee with plain T5 and T6 bodies and re-run the test boards.

assumptions.assumption: No tribe needs its own way to turn gold into stats.
assumptions.evidence_for: The neutral spells Pinch of Dust and Last Orders exist for everyone.
assumptions.evidence_against: Bog has no such route. Birds' route is rate-limited. Only Hedgerow's compounds.
assumptions.test: Round-12 and round-16 test boards that spend surplus gold through each tribe's route.

motivations.player_wants: Replay When played text, and grow Birds while they are away, then cash them in.
motivations.tension: An away Bird fights as a half-stat Egg with no text. Homecoming cards end the trips the Cuckoo is growing.

motivations.system: The Cuckoo, Redwing, the Great Lump and the Gabble Ratchet
motivations.player_wants: One huge Bird expressed in full.
motivations.tension: Redwing and the Cuckoo need the same same-row slot next to the Nest, and the pile shows at full size only for a moment in combat.

motivations.player_wants: Pick the matchups, and grow walls that hold the enemy carry.
motivations.tension: Every payoff needs the enemy to attack into you, and most gains vanish after the fight. Permanent growth is limited to once or twice a fight.

motivations.player_wants: Turn slots into power, and fill empty slots with Wisps.
motivations.tension: The +4/+4 cap stops a slot from holding a carry, and empty slots compete with having a full board.

motivations.player_wants: Early support growth, then a cash-out for gold and Rings.
motivations.tension: Shy units can't be buffed, so they become dead weight. The cash-out happens once.

motivations.player_wants: Concentrate the board's stats into one Fairy.
motivations.tension: She splits evenly among every other Fairy, so concentrating means dropping Fairy Monarch and Supper's tribe-wide value. She destroys your own units.

motivations.player_wants: An economy lead that becomes a stat lead.
motivations.tension: No other tribe gives the same loop; their economy cards pay gold that no tribal card spends.

owner_questions.question: Should flying cost half a Bird's stats in combat?
owner_questions.why: Every Hatchery payoff (Cuckoo, Lump, Redwing, Ratchet) is diluted by half-stat Eggs. Birds are last in the lobbies, and their biggest board at round 9 still loses. This is an identity call about whether a Bird is still defending its Nest while away.
owner_questions.default_answer: Eggs fight at full Health and half Attack by default. Tom Tit gives full Attack instead. Golden Tom Tit adds +2/+2.

owner_questions.question: Is Bog the answer tribe, beating big boards by shrinking them rather than building its own big unit?
owner_questions.why: Its design already points that way (Bufo's halving; Snap and Lantern Man aim at the biggest stuck enemy), but its flat debuffs weaken as stat scale rises, and its permanent growth is tiny.
owner_questions.default_answer: Yes. Turn flat debuffs into proportional ones as numbers rise (Bitter takes a share of Attack, Jenny takes a quarter), and give Bog one real pile: Ranocchio twice a fight.

owner_questions.question: Should Fairy power stay spread across slots, or may a Ring slot hold a carry?
owner_questions.why: The +4/+4 cap leaves the Queen as the only Fairy concentrator, and she fights the rest of the tribe.
owner_questions.default_answer: Keep Rings as the identity, but raise the cap to +2/+2 per shop tier (+12/+12 at tier 6). Let the Queen give her whole share to one Fairy you choose.

owner_questions.question: Should every tribe have its own way to turn spare gold into stats, as Acorns do for Hedgerow?
owner_questions.why: Only Hedgerow's economy lead becomes a stat lead. The owner's note says rewards give power, and Battlegrounds stats grow through economy.
owner_questions.default_answer: Yes, one per tribe, each with its own condition. Example: each Mrs Stork return also gives that Bird +1/+1; Peat Cutter gold can be spent on a Bog grower.

maps.summary:
I audited 48 tribe cards (16 each for Hedgerow, Hunters and Oozes) and 13 neutrals. Full per-card table: /tmp/claude-1000/-home-alex-code-Bramble-ideation/5369878e-e379-478d-ac97-3201f49297d2/scratchpad/fundamentals/card-audit-hedgerow-hunters-oozes.md.

Hedgerow stands apart in four ways:
- It has the most permanent payoffs (8 of 13; Hunters have 3 of 13).
- Its growth fires in the Recruit Phase, so it grows without winning fights.
- Pass piles stats onto one unit.
- Committee and Lollop are full-board fight auras that any gapless board satisfies and any tribe can run.

In bot play, Hedgerow's lead is mostly one card. 70 of 71 Hedgerow wins had Squire Lollop. 206 of the 336 winners in lobbies that included Hedgerow had Lollop. Hedgerow does not have more stats than Hunters (round 12 per-unit 20.6 vs 21.4). The Hoard route and Alderman Dozey are barely played: larder p90 is 2 gold, and Dozey does not predict wins. So the owner's claim that Hedgerow's strength shows the other tribes are too weak is incomplete.

Hunters' payoffs nearly all reset after each fight (10 of 13). The few permanent ones need fight wins and give at most one Take a fight. Oozes' power sits mostly in enablers and in Belly reserves that the bench does not count.

Owner claims checked:
- Numbers are too small: right. Typical round-16 boards are about 13/14 a unit, and every fast single-unit grower is capped (Dozey +12/+12, Treasurer +8/+8, Supper +3/+3, Ring +4/+4).
- Concentration beats spread: incomplete under our rules. Pack, Pounce and quarry focus let spread units hit one target together, and the pool has many answers to one big unit.
- Shape of the curve: the bot curve is very narrow (round 12 p99/p50 = 1.43). Bots under-play greedy lines, so this is a floor, not a verdict.

owner_questions.question: Should Squire Lollop and the Standing Committee buff only Hedgerow folk ('Hedgerow folk touching this'), or stay full-board buffs that any tribe can use?
owner_questions.why: They decide most bot games in any tribe (206 of 336 winners where Hedgerow is in the lobby). They blur tribe identity and make Hedgerow's measured strength mostly one card's strength. This is a question of taste, not measurement.
owner_questions.default_answer: Make both Hedgerow-only, as Goodman Hayward already is. Keep the full-board bonus. Give the neutral pool its own late card for any tribe.

owner_questions.question: Should we remove the hard ceilings on the units that grow fastest (Dozey +12/+12, Treasurer +8/+8) and rely on answers in the pool (Sergeant, Ichneumon Wasp, Hasty Pudding, Whirligig) to beat a big carry?
owner_questions.why: They are the only fast single-unit growers, so the caps remove the rare-highroll tail the owner wants. Whether a capped carry is good design is a call for a designer.
owner_questions.default_answer: Remove both ceilings. Keep Dozey's single double. If constructed sims show the carry is common rather than rare, limit how often it can grow (e.g. feeding once a turn) rather than how big it gets.

owner_questions.question: Is a tribe whose power is almost all fight-only (Hunters) a good identity, or should every tribe have at least one permanent growth line?
owner_questions.why: Hunters grow almost nothing between turns, and their late win share falls. The owner wants rewards that make the player feel stronger.
owner_questions.default_answer: Give Hunters one permanent line at T5: the Mountain Glutton keeps its first Take's +2/+2 each fight permanently. Keep the rest fight-only.

maps.summary: Battlegrounds stats grow exponentially from turn 8. Bramble's grow in a straight line. I measured BG from a 2026 game data source no Bramble doc had used yet: Firestone's public per-turn board averages (288,790 games in the current patch, plus archived snapshots back to Sep 2025) and 150 replays I parsed (129 valid). In the current patch an ordinary BG board has a median of 24 stats at turn 4, 62 at turn 6, 149 at turn 8, 714 at turn 10, 2,598 at turn 12 and 7,980 at turn 14. That is about x1.9 per turn after turn 8. Bramble bots: 30, 52, 80, 107, 133, 155. The early game matches; the gap opens at turn 7-8. The curve depends on the patch: the turn-12 mean went from 759 (Sep 2025) to 3,505 (Nov 2026). Top-1% players have about 1.8x the mean board. BG's growth comes from compounding text: 25% of the pool says 'this game', 'improve' or 'extra'. Bramble's slice has one such card. The tail: from turn 8, 13-23% of ordinary BG boards are at least 2x the median. The top 0.4% of games run 2-3x the median, and their top tenth 7-18x. In 400 bot lobbies no Bramble board ever reached 2x the median. In BG the biggest unit holds about a third of the board's stats in every turn. Yet in 14-26% of fights the side that won had fewer stats. Concentration helps vanilla bodies, but summons, keywords and scam break it. The VOD route works (readable 720p frames) but costs about 3 minutes and 12-20 image reads a game, and the turn index is fragile. Replays are far better for BG; Galaxy needs VODs.

findings.claim: Per-turn BG board totals, current patch (Nov 2026), ordinary players: median (p10-p90) T4 24 (11-40), T6 62 (38-85), T8 149 (83-343), T10 714 (249-1,565), T12 2,598 (629-6,572), T14 7,980 (2,102-31,933). Confidence high to T12, medium at T14 (n=60, survivors only).

findings.claim: The gap comes from compounding text, not from printed stats or tier budgets. BG's printed buffs are also small; its growth comes from second-order text that makes later buffs bigger. Bramble's slice has almost none of it, and most of its growth is capped.
findings.evidence: docs/research/battlegrounds/data/minions.csv, current solo pool, regex in scripts/bg_buff_sizes.py; Bramble content/units/*.json with set 'slice'.
findings.numbers: BG: 68 of 273 minions (25%) have 'this game', 'improve', 'extra', 'for each' or 'equal to' text. Median buff in text by tier: +2, +2, +3, +4, +6, +4.5 (Attack plus Health). Bramble: 1 of 119 slice cards is second-order (Fairy Monarch). Buffs are +1/+1 or +2/+2 at every tier. The two largest are +8/+8 caps (Alderman Dozey, Honorary Treasurer). About 7 cards grow permanently, in +1/+1 steps, mostly capped per fight or per turn.

findings.claim: Shape of the curve. In BG the tail opens at turn 8 and widens every turn. The top 0.4% of games (no damage taken) reach 10x the ordinary median, as the owner expected. Bramble bots have no tail at all.
findings.evidence: scripts/shape.py; shape.txt. Perfect games are about 0.36% of uploaded games: 1,000 in 5.5 days against about 51,000 games a day.
findings.numbers: BG ordinary boards at least 2x the median: T6 1%, T8 13%, T10 14%, T12 23%, T14 23%. At least 3x: 3%, 4%, 9%, 18% (T8-T14). p90/p50: 1.4 (T6) up to 4.0 (T14). Top-0.4% winners, as a multiple of the ordinary median: median 2.0x at T10, 3.0x at T12; p90 6.6x at T10, 11.7x at T12, 17.7x at T14. Bramble: 0% of boards at 2x the median in any round; p90/p50 1.21-1.32; max/median 1.7-2.0.

findings.claim: Concentration. BG boards keep about a third of their stats in the biggest unit at every turn, for ordinary players and winners alike. Winners are not more concentrated than losers, and fewer stats often still win.
findings.evidence: Replay combats (underdog.txt, tall_wide.txt) and the final boards of all 1,000 perfect games (perfect_final.txt).
findings.numbers: Biggest-unit share, median: 0.32-0.35 for ordinary boards and 0.33-0.36 for winners (T6-T15; an even board would be 0.14). The side that took no damage had fewer stats in 14-26% of fights and less than half in 1-8%. Beast Beetles won at T14 with 194 stats against 6,666. A unit holding at least 60% of its board: 7% of ordinary boards, 12% of winners' boards. Tall-against-wide fights are 7% of fights from T8. Final stats of winning comps span 35x: Demon shop 36,373 down to Beast Beetle 1,088.

findings.claim: Skill moves the curve by about 1.8x, so bots will understate what skilled players produce.

findings.numbers: 0 units at 2.147 billion; 4 units over 1 million; 19 of 1,000 games (1.9%) had a unit over 100,000.

assumptions.assumption: The power budget prices printed stats and first-order effects per tier. Compounding (buffs that make later buffs bigger) is neither priced nor designed for, so the content cannot produce BG's late-game curve.

assumptions.evidence_against: In 14-26% of BG fights the side with fewer stats won. Deathrattle and keyword comps win with up to 35x fewer stats.

owner_questions.question: Which BG era's curve should Bramble aim for: Sep 2025 (median board about 300 at T10, 750 at T12, 1,750 at T14) or the current one (about 700, 2,600, 8,000)?
owner_questions.why: Content density of 'improve this game' engines and the late-game numbers all follow from this target. A measurement can't pick the taste.
owner_questions.default_answer: Sep 2025-like: about x1.5 per turn after T8, carries around 100/100 by T12, with 4-digit totals only in highroll games.

owner_questions.question: Is a BG-like tail the target? That means 15-25% of boards at least 2x the median at T10-12, and the top 1% at about 10x.
owner_questions.why: This sets how much uncapped compounding each tribe gets and what reviewers should flag.
owner_questions.default_answer: Yes: aim for p90/p50 of 2-2.5 at T10-12 and treat 10x outliers below 1% of games as fine.

owner_questions.question: Should every tribe get at least one uncapped compounding engine (a 'this game' or 'improve' effect) at tier 3-5, or only some tribes, with others winning through scam, width or keywords?
owner_questions.why: In BG the winning comps span 35x in stats, so both routes work. Choosing one decides the pass-3 content brief.
owner_questions.default_answer: Every tribe gets one compounding engine. Two tribes also get a strong non-stat win route (scam or width), as Murlocs and Beetles have in BG.

owner_questions.question: What game length should a winner target?
owner_questions.why: Bramble winners last a median 20 rounds against BG's 13-15. Growth rate and the damage curve both depend on it.
owner_questions.default_answer: Winners finish by round 14-16.

motivations.player_wants: To feel stronger every turn and chase a highroll; numbers that jump are the reward.
