motivations.player_wants: A way to beat bigger numbers with clever play.
motivations.tension: They break stat-total metrics: BG winners with 1/30 of the opponent's stats. Budgets that count stats will misjudge them.

maps.summary: Our process keeps fixing whole-game problems one card at a time. From 7 to 9 Nov, at least 19 decisions (DECISIONS.md) added a cap, a limiter or a dearer climb after something dominated. 22% of the 109 pool units now carry a cap or limiter; by our own taxonomy, Battlegrounds limiters sit at about 5%. The cause is built in. The power budget treats stats as additive and growth as linear, and it gives cut power to per-tier growth caps. Designers work without the budget, but a costing reviewer applies it with veto power, by hand, with no simulations. It made 10 cuts in pass 2, all taken, and every costing-versus-triage split went its way. The bot that serves as our per-tribe bar (the plain free-choice arm) has three blind spots. It values card text at 1.5 × tier, so within a tier it ranks units by printed stats. Every seat climbs on one fixed curve. It almost never saves gold. In 400 lobbies, gold left was ≥5 in under 10% of turns, and tier 4 came at round 8–9 for 80% of seats. Changeling and Ichneumon Wasp were on 0 of 3,200 final boards, so answers to a big unit never get tested. Fairies, the tribe with the lowest early stats, were picked by 0.9% of seats but took first in 31% of those games. So bot lobbies can't measure how often snowballs happen, what engines are worth, or whether answers work. Bots plan placement against the next opponent's last-round board, never buy against it, and never predict changes. The ghost is a frozen, fully known board, but only 3% of fights are against it. Nobody owns the stat scale, the bot's valuation model, or whether the bars measure the game rather than the bot. Pass 2 is already merged into ideation/main (97f8d49).

findings.claim: Systemic problems got local fixes again and again: caps, limiters and a dearer climb after each dominance.
findings.evidence: DECISIONS.md lines: 564 (bot curves slowed by hand, 'tempo beats tiers'; HARD_CURVE comment at src/core/bots/bot_level.gd:20-21), 586 (Dozey +8/+8, Hex -8), 601/622 (Mast), 624-625 (5→6 climb costs 13 'provisional… hand play decides'; still 13 at src/core/game_config.gd:21), 631 (Partner), 527 (Pie), 499-501 (Hoard 16, Treasurer +8/+8), 496 (Money Spider), 475/708 (Dozey +12/+12), 322 (Whistlers 1/1), 298-306 (Burner cap and tier move), 295 (Bird bot priors cut), 159 (Ring +4/+4), 128/158 (Hex ≤ tier), 130/151 (Chaser), 152-154 (Toll-Bard, Bracken, Spider), 76-121 (pass 2's 10 costing cuts), 10/44/47 (Toad, Peat Cutter). The orchestrator's own line 27: 'Caps added after each dominance… treated a system problem as card problems.'
findings.numbers: At least 19 entries over 7–9 Nov. 24 of 109 slice-pool units (22%) carry an explicit cap or limiter, 17 of them (16%) per-turn or per-fight limiters. Our taxonomy puts Battlegrounds limiters at 5% of the pool (power-budget.md:224).

findings.claim: The power budget forbids the compounding the owner asks for, and the costing reviewer enforces it as a veto, by hand.
findings.evidence: power-budget.md:205-206: 'Linear growth only… Stat multiply and consume grow geometrically… priced only when the text is once per turn and can't be retriggered'. power-budget.md:125 sets per-tier growth caps. pass2-costing.md:3 says 'Hand estimates, no sims', and most of its 10 cuts are 'growth above the per-tier caps'. DECISIONS:76 says all 10 were taken. All three costing-versus-triage splits went to costing (DECISIONS:45, 98, 112).
findings.numbers: Growth caps of 0.8/1.3/1.7/2.5/3.8 SP a turn for T1–T5. V(t) = 5/7/8/10/12/14 SP, so a par T3 is 8 SP, a 4/4: below the owner's 'very low' 5/5 example. The scale target is '13/13 by turn 12' (DECISIONS:792), and the budget assumes 180-SP turn-12 boards (power-budget.md:203). Bot medians: 10/10 per unit at R12.

findings.claim: Bots value stats as additive and have no time horizon, so engines and answers are hidden. The plain arm, which is the tribe bar, ranks units by printed stats.
findings.evidence: bot_eval.gd:36-91: keep = Attack + Health + a flat hint (or 1.5 × tier); no round or turns-left input anywhere in BotEval. tools/sim/plain_eval.gd replaces every keep/buy hint with 1.5 × tier. The only modelled horizon is Grizel's fixed 2.5 fights (bot_carrier.gd:159). Ranking within a tier is in scratchpad plain_rank.txt. The owner's example, a T3 2/2 that gains +1/+1 at End of Turn, values 8.5 against a 5/5's 14.5, and still loses after it reaches 5/5 because of the replace margin of 3.
findings.numbers: On final boards in 400 plain lobbies: Changeling 0/3,200, Ichneumon Wasp 0/3,200, Money Spider 0.1%, Old Moth Annis 0.5%, Hob 0.1%, Fairy Monarch 0.5% (holders' mean place 1.67, n=15), Laird 3.2% (2.65).

findings.claim: Bot planning failures shaped the caps both ways. Engines that pay off with no planning ran away and got capped; engines that need planning read as weak.
findings.evidence: Runaway automatic engines: Dozey on 70–96% of final boards (DECISIONS:579), Mast with Treasury winning 44.6% (601). Planned engines read as dead: Burner had 1 buyer in 240 seats and 0 gold burned (298); a Stash was held in 19 of 4,475 player-turns (833); the reactive-saving bot failed at +0.0475 ±0.086 and the Acorn Stash bot at +0.011 ±0.045 (BOTS.md). triage-audit §4: the answers 'Changeling and Whirligig… bots never use them'.
findings.numbers: Bot improvements so far: carrier +0.048 ±0.042 places, the only promotion.

findings.claim: In the plain arm every seat follows one scripted tier curve and spends nearly all its gold, so bot lobbies can't produce or measure greed-driven snowballs.
findings.evidence: free_choice.gd sets strategy {}, so _target_round falls back to HARD_CURVE [4,7,9,12,14]. Climbs are valued at 100 and always happen when due (bot_brain.gd:237-280). There are no save tables. Tables are in the scratchpad file bots_lobby_tables.txt.
findings.numbers: Mean gold left is 0.2–1.8 every round; gold left ≥5 in at most 9.9% of seat-turns (R9). First round at tier 4: p10 8, p50 9, p90 9 (sd 0.52). Tier 6: p50 14, reached by only 49% of seats. The lobby leader's board against the lobby median at R12: p50 1.22, p99 1.60, max 1.63.

findings.claim: The free-choice tribe bar tracks the bot's valuation more than the tribe. Pick rates follow printed early stats, and the two arms disagree wildly.
findings.evidence: free_choice_plain.summary.csv against printed stats by tier from content/units. DECISIONS:67: Birds picked 21.1% in the plain arm, 1.3% in the hinted arm. DECISIONS:13: Birds first went from 13.5% to 4.9% between runs, so 'the Birds bar is met' no longer holds.
findings.numbers: Hunters (T1 mean 4.7 stats) picked by 22.0% of seats. Fairies (T1 3.0, T2 4.0) picked by 0.9%, first in 31% of their 29 seats. 37% of seats end with no tribe.

findings.claim: The owner's 'early game decides' worry is half right on bot data: an early record decides top 4, not the winner.
findings.evidence: rounds.csv results for R1–6 joined to players.csv place. 3,200 seats, all alive through R6.
findings.numbers: Top 4 by early losses: 0 losses 88%, 1 loss 73%, 3 losses 46%, 5 losses 29%. First place stays at 13–19% for 0–3 losses. 45.5% of lobby winners lost 3 or more of their first 6 fights. Caveat: every seat is on one curve, so no bot trades early losses for greed.

findings.claim: Scouting and ghosts: against live bots the information is symmetric; the ghost is fully known and frozen but rare. Bots don't adapt buys to the next opponent.
findings.evidence: game_session.gd:672-706: everyone gets the next opponent's last fought board, slots, hero and tier. The reveal rule is off (DECISIONS:418, 464). Bots use the scout for placement (a 20-fight search when the stat ratio is 0.6–1.7, bot_placer.gd:64-76, 418-450), a ±1 tier shift, flights, Peat King and Horseshoe; never for buys, and they never predict the opponent's re-placement. Generic carries are pinned as 'landmarks for the next opponent's scout' (bot_placer.gd:453-460), which makes bots easy for a human to read. Ghost: the last eliminated player's board, no hero, never changes, deals damage (game_session.gd:853-869).
findings.numbers: Ghost fights are 1,461 of 48,773 player-fights (3.0%), about 3.65 rounds per lobby. Placement value against the exact board: +23.8 points; against a decoy (the scout-like case): +6.4 (DECISIONS:230). By eye, readers gained +1.9 without one obvious screen (DECISIONS:464).

findings.claim: The constructed R9 bench is the closest thing we have to the owner's 'empirical simulation at turn thresholds', but it removes economy and compounding by construction.
findings.evidence: pass2-followup-boards.md:3-11: hand ledgers at 62 ±3 net gold, one growth layer each, no T6, heroes ignored. pass2-benchmark-results.md: cells mostly 0% or 100%. review-pass2-followup.md:9: one extra +1/+1 per unit moves boards 22–68 points.
findings.numbers: 13,200 fights run in minutes. 12 boards (6 tribes × high/low), all by one hand.

findings.claim: Delegation leaves the whole game unowned, and the agents that judge designs can't run experiments.
findings.evidence: DECISIONS:25: no Godot in workflow agents. Sims run only through Sol builders, so costing is by hand. Builders change bot hints without a plan line (review-pass2-followup ask 3: Toad 4→6, Committee 14→12). Scope reviewers judge one commit range against the orchestrator's plan. Hints are tuned to make cards get bought (content/bots/README.md: 'These values let their text compete with early buffed bodies'). The placing bar and the bot-promotion floor were both rewritten after results (DECISIONS:243-247).
findings.numbers: One scope review per merge in most entries (damage-b, feedback5, pass 2 follow-up). Design passes get 2 paper reviews, no sims.

findings.claim: The tally's must-fix rule turned a natural property of the genre into a defect list.
findings.evidence: triage-audit.md §1: row 3, 'One huge unit or stat pile decides games' (11 reports), and row 5, Ring piles (7), became must-fixes under rule E and led to the caps. The owner's 9a/9d: concentrating stats is always better without scam, and the answer to a big unit is scam, not a cap.
findings.numbers: 11 + 7 + 6 (Chaser) reports, all fixed with caps or bounds.

assumptions.assumption: Stats are additive: 1 Attack = 1 Health = 1 SP, and a 20/20 is worth two 10/10s.
assumptions.where: power-budget.md SP unit; bot_eval.gd:36-55; bot_brain.gd:270-279 (pressure by stat sum)
assumptions.evidence_for: Simple and costable; the fight engine handles distribution in placement search.
assumptions.evidence_against: Owner 9a (3×10/11 beats 5×10/10) and 9d (one 2.1B unit is easier to beat than three 500M). The +1/+1 probe swings 22–68 points.
assumptions.test: Constructed fights: equal-SP boards with concentrated and spread stats at R6/R9/R12, with and without an answer unit.

assumptions.assumption: Growth should be linear and capped per tier; compounding is allowed only once a turn without retriggers.
assumptions.evidence_for: It stopped measured runaways (Dozey, Mast).
assumptions.evidence_against: Owner 9a: healthy Battlegrounds boards reach 100/100 or more. Bot medians are 10/10 at R12. The runaways were measured by bots that never buy answers.
assumptions.test: Scale experiments: lift the caps on 3–4 engines and fight constructed R9/R12 boards that include answer units.

assumptions.assumption: The plain free-choice lobby is a valid per-tribe bar.
assumptions.evidence_for: It removes hand-set hints, so routing can't hide a weak tribe.
assumptions.evidence_against: Text at 1.5 × tier, one curve, no saving; Changeling and Wasp 0/3,200; Fairies 0.9% picked but 31% first; Birds first 13.5% → 4.9% between runs.
assumptions.test: Re-run with an engine-aware valuation and a greed curve; if tribe ranks reorder, the bar measures the bot.

assumptions.assumption: Designers briefed without the budget produce novel designs that survive.
assumptions.evidence_for: Pass 2 docs did contain new growth engines (Lollop, Mallow, Beadle).
assumptions.evidence_against: The costing reviewer cut 10 of them against linear caps, all taken, and won every split, so the budget comes back as a veto.
assumptions.test: Count how many designer-original texts reach the build unchanged in pass 2 against pass 1.

assumptions.assumption: Buy-moment costing: each card must be a sensible pick on its own when bought.
assumptions.evidence_for: It caught the Birds early-game trap.
assumptions.evidence_against: It penalises condition-and-payoff engines that are worse now and better in 3 turns (the owner's 2/2 +1/+1 example).
assumptions.test: Cost engines over their expected hold time (turns kept, from bot or constructed data), not at the moment of purchase.

assumptions.assumption: Three or more playtest reports make a must-fix.
assumptions.evidence_for: Recurring problems (Birds, clarity) stopped being ignored.
assumptions.evidence_against: Concentration complaints (11 reports) became caps; agent playtesters are not elite players.
assumptions.test: Classify each tally row as a defect, a missing answer, or a taste call before it counts.

assumptions.assumption: Card-count parity of 16 at 3/3/3/3/2/2 makes tribe competition fair.
assumptions.evidence_for: The owner asked for it (08f), and it removes supply skew.
assumptions.evidence_against: Tiers were moved to fit the count (Figgy, Burner, Money Spider); neutrals (13) and spells sit outside it.
assumptions.test: Measure per-window useful-card density per tribe in constructed shops.

assumptions.assumption: Bots that are tuned after bench results are still a neutral instrument.
assumptions.evidence_for: The tuning is logged honestly.
assumptions.evidence_against: Curves were slowed when 'tempo beat tiers'; Bird priors were cut to steer away from weak routes; hints were raised so cards get bought.
assumptions.test: Freeze the bots during a measurement pass; report results under two bot variants.

assumptions.assumption: Fixed R9 boards at a common 62 ±3 gold spend are fair benchmarks.
assumptions.evidence_for: It stopped the fixtures measuring spend.
assumptions.evidence_against: It also removes economy and compounding advantages, the owner's main concern; no T6; results are near 0% or 100%.
assumptions.test: Add boards with different spend at the same round (an economy line against a tempo line), and generated rather than hand-built boards.

assumptions.assumption: One fresh scope reviewer per merge, judging against the orchestrator's plan, is enough independence.
assumptions.where: PLAN.md:91; CLOUD.md 'How a cloud reviewer reviews'
assumptions.evidence_for: It caught real cuts (soak Toad gold, Wasp Last Blow).
assumptions.evidence_against: No reviewer saw the caps pile up across steps; the follow-up review said it 'moves the original problem: a little'.
assumptions.test: A periodic whole-game critic that reads all DECISIONS since the last one.

assumptions.assumption: Bot head-to-head gains are evidence of bot strength.
assumptions.evidence_for: Paired seeds and an A/A check are sound statistics.
assumptions.evidence_against: It compares a bot only with bots that can't plan either; gains are about 0.05 places.
assumptions.test: Compare against scripted expert lines in constructed scenarios (bank-then-spike, triple hunts).

assumptions.assumption: Agents that judge designs don't need to run the engine.
assumptions.where: DECISIONS:25 (no Godot in workflow agents); CLOUD.md
assumptions.evidence_for: The machine is memory-limited.
assumptions.evidence_against: Costing becomes paper SP math; constructed sims are cheap (13,200 fights in minutes).
assumptions.test: Give critics a queued sim service (Sol runs, critic specifies the boards).

assumptions.assumption: Bot lobby data can say how often snowballs happen.
assumptions.where: implicit in DECISIONS:27 (the 'biggest board is 1.2× median' argument)
assumptions.evidence_for: Large samples.
assumptions.evidence_against: One curve, gold left ≥5 in under 10% of turns, no greed line; the leader against the median is p99 1.60.
assumptions.test: A policy family (tempo, greed, fast tier, roll-down) in mixed lobbies; compare the tail shape.

owner_questions.question: For constructed sims, what should a strong player have at R6, R9 and R12 on an average, high and low roll: tier, gold spent and triples?
owner_questions.why: Constructed setups need a reference curve. Our bots reach tier 4 at R9 and tier 6 at R14, so bot data can't supply one. You can give it from Battlegrounds experience faster than we can measure it.
owner_questions.default_answer: Average: T3 by R4–5, T4 by R6–7, T5 by R8–9, T6 by R10–11, one triple by R7 and 2–3 by R11. High roll: one round earlier plus one triple. Low roll: one round later, no triple by R9.

owner_questions.question: What snowball frequency is acceptable?
owner_questions.why: You said the shape matters, not the top 1%. We need a target to test against.
owner_questions.default_answer: In at most 25% of lobbies the winner held the top board from R6 onward. At least 20% of winners were below the lobby median at R8. Top-1% boards may reach 5–10 times the median.

owner_questions.question: Should 'one huge unit decides games' stop counting as a must-fix?
owner_questions.why: It drove most of our caps. Your view is that concentration is natural and answers are the counter.
owner_questions.default_answer: Yes. Treat it as a test instead: at that round, a common board with an answer unit must beat the big carry at least 30% of the time. If none can, add or strengthen answers, not caps.

owner_questions.question: Should the costing reviewer advise rather than veto?
owner_questions.why: It cut 10 of 10 in pass 2 by hand math against linear caps.
owner_questions.default_answer: Advise only. It can cut when a constructed sim at the card's window shows a common-roll board with the card winning at least 80% against same-round peers, or when the card makes an unbounded loop. Everything else is a watch item.

owner_questions.question: Do we stop bot strength work at 'okay' and build a small family of fixed play styles as the sanity check?
owner_questions.why: You say bots will never be elite. Our promotion campaigns have gained about 0.05 places each.
owner_questions.default_answer: Yes. Player-facing Hard stays as it is, plus fixes so it values engines, answers and saving. The sanity check uses 4–5 parameterised styles (tempo, greed economy, fast tier, roll-down, answers) in mixed lobbies. No more head-to-head promotion runs.

motivations.system: Bot valuation: Attack + Health + a flat text hint, with no horizon
motivations.player_wants: the biggest stats now
motivations.tension: Engines and answers are never bought, so lobby bars favour tribes with high printed early stats and hide payoff tribes (Fairies picked 0.9%, first in 31% of those seats).

motivations.system: Buy-moment costing and per-tier growth caps
motivations.player_wants: a card that is a sensible pick on the turn it's bought
motivations.tension: It conflicts with condition-and-payoff engines that are worse now and better later, which is the reward loop the owner wants.

motivations.system: Scout of the next opponent's last-round board, plus a bot placement search
motivations.player_wants: to counter-place against what they saw
motivations.tension: The bot assumes the opponent won't change and keeps its carry fixed as a landmark, so a human can read and exploit it. The bot never buys against the scout.

motivations.system: One tier curve and spending all gold for every free-choice seat
motivations.player_wants: to keep up on tempo
motivations.tension: Nobody greeds, so early losses only ever mean being behind. Bots can't show the economy-to-tempo snowball, so its frequency can't be measured from lobbies.

motivations.system: Playtest tally rule E (3+ reports is a must-fix)
motivations.player_wants: no single unit deciding the game
motivations.tension: It turns concentration, which the genre naturally has, into a cap list instead of a call for answers.

critics.verdict: The maps are right that Bramble is a straight-line game built on printed stats. Income matches Battlegrounds, but late gold buys about 1 stat, one card in 119 compounds, and 22% of units carry a cap. Under our rules "too small" is not a scale problem. Fights are counts of exchanges decided by breakpoints, so stat totals mislead every tool we have, and multiplying stats changes only granularity and the bite of flat effects. The rework needs four things. First, one target for growth per round and game length together: x1.5 a round over our 20-round games is about 90x. Second, compounding channels every tribe can use: the capped tribe bonus, spells, the shop. Third, answers that can reach a back-row carry. Fourth, a variance budget, because our near-deterministic fights would turn any compounding curve into common snowballs. To measure how often a board happens, not just how strong it is: goldfish rollouts of strong scripted lines through the real shop, then fights between populations of boards, then scripted-line lobbies with real damage. Bot-lobby findings are weak, and the R9 fixtures mostly measure breakpoints. The owner's claims hold for BG's scale and for fewer, bigger bodies. "Always concentrate" and "a giant is easy to scam" need keywords and answers we don't have.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: Total stats (Attack + Health) measure a board's strength, so costing, the bot's buy score and the bench can just add stats up.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: Our fights are counts of exchanges. Each side attacks once a turn, overkill is lost, and a unit lasts ceil(Health ÷ enemy Attack) hits. Crossing the enemy's breakpoints is what wins, so the same total wins anywhere from 0% to 100% depending on how it is split.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: 3×10/11 beat 5×10/10 in 5,600 of 5,600 fights. 65 stats as six 5/6s win 96.5%; the same total as 5/6 front and 6/5 back wins 64.7%. A carry plus small units wins 0-15% at equal totals. +1/+1 on every unit moves R9 boards 22-68 points. Brother Bracken (5 units, up to +5/+5) is the best hero, mean place 2.70.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: In the real engine, fit a strength measure from the exchange model (hits each unit survives against the enemy's Attack, kills per hit) on constructed boards at R6, R9, R12 and R16. If it predicts fights better than totals, use it in costing, in the bot's valuation and in the bench logs.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: With bot lobbies demoted, a few hand-built boards per tribe at one round can stand in for the game.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: A fixed board tells you how strong a board is once built, not how often it gets built, and the owner is asking how often. Ours are 12 boards by one hand, all at R9 with the same gold, no tier 6 and no economy. Their cells sit at 0% or 100% and move 22-68 points on +1/+1.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: r9-results.md; 59 of 66 plain pairs fall outside 10-90%; review-pass2-followup.md:9.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: Goldfish rollouts: for each tribe, script 2-3 lines a strong player would take (tempo, fast tier, economy, tribe engine) turn by turn. Run each through the real shop and pool with 500+ seeds, and snapshot start-of-combat boards, held bodies included, at R6/8/10/12/14/16. Then fight sampled boards against a sampled field, not one board against one.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: 'Numbers too small' is fixed with bigger numbers: bigger printed bodies, a steeper tier curve, a target like 50/50 by R12.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: Multiplying every stat by k leaves fights unchanged: +10% stats is worth about 15 points at any scale. BG's printed buffs are small too (median +2 to +6). Its curve comes from text that makes each later gold buy more stats, and we have almost none. A bigger scale only makes steps finer and flat effects smaller.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: scale.txt: +10% stays at 15-19 points for k = 1, 2 and 4, while the +1/+1 swing falls from 30 to 9 points at k = 4. Stats per gold spent so far: Bramble 1.5 at R8 and 1.4 at R14; BG 2.8, 9.9, 28 and 71 at T8/10/12/14. 68 of 273 BG minions have 'this game', 'improve' or 'extra' text; 1 of 119 Bramble cards is second-order.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: Write the scale spec as growth per round after R8, spread (p90/p50 at R10-12) and stats per gold by round, not as unit sizes. Test it by giving each tribe one uncapped 'this game' engine in the goldfish rollouts.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: Compounding can be added while combat stays as deterministic as it is now.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: Our fights follow the stat ratio closely. On a x1.5-a-round curve, one round of tempo makes a 1.5x board, which wins 94%. Streaks then become runaways: the common snowball the owner doesn't want. BG keeps upsets alive with scam, shields, deathrattles and targets anywhere on the board. Our back-row protection and across-aimed answers remove most of that variance.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: Bramble: a board at 1.5x+ the median wins 94%, rank 1 wins 76-79%, and the chance of a win is 60.3% after a win and 41.0% after a loss. BG: the perfect-game winner had fewer stats than its opponent in 14-26% of its fights at every turn.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: After adding engines, measure in the population fights how win rate follows the stat ratio, and the share of R10-14 fights the smaller board wins. Add variance (answers that ignore rows, summons, shields) until that share reaches the owner's target.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: Caps and per-tier growth limits are what keep runaways in check.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: The runaways that led to the caps were measured with bots that never field answers, and costed by hand. Caps cut off the rare highroll tail the owner wants. 22% of our units now carry one, against about 5% in BG.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: Dozey at 96/94 was on 70-96% of final boards before his cap, while Changeling and Ichneumon Wasp were on 0 of 3,200. All 10 pass-2 costing cuts were taken, and 19 cap decisions were made from 7 to 9 Nov.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: Uncap Dozey, the Treasurer, Rings, Supper and the Toad in the goldfish rollouts. Measure the tail (p99/p50) and whether a common board with one answer beats each uncapped carry at least 30% of the time at its round. Where it can't, add a rate limit or an answer, not a size cap.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: The pool already has enough answers to make big carries fair.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: Most answers hit 'the enemy across', so they need the layouts to line up, and back-row protection keeps a B3 carry out of reach until the front row dies. The flat answers shrink as stats grow. There is no venom and no 'destroy the biggest'. None has been tested in play, because bots never take them.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: Dozey in B3 wins 96.4%, against 83.9% in F1. Sergeant deals 3 damage a gold, Jack Daw takes 2, Bitter 1-2, Hex up to your tier. Model: Nightshade on Dozey −28.5 points; venom on one front unit −12.2.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: An answer matrix: each answer card against carry boards at R12 and R16, with the carry in B3 and in the front row, and the answer's owner placed both against the scouted board and blind. Record each answer's swing.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: The damage rule needs no change for the scale rework.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: Damage sets the price of greed and how fast a winner closes the game. Early losses cost 1-4 Health, and late damage is mostly the round base, so how hard you win barely matters. Once gold buys compounding stats, greed becomes cheap. Game length and growth rate are also linked: in 20-round games, x1.5 a round from R8 grows boards about 90x.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: Losing all of R1-6 leaves about 25 of 40 Health. From R12, survivors are 11-16% of a loss. Winners play 19.5 rounds; BG perfect games end at a median turn 14.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: A scripted-line lobby: 8 seats, each running a line from the goldfish set, with real fights and the real damage rule. Measure the greed line's Health at R10, game length, and how often the R8 leader wins. Then set base damage and Health for the target length.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: Tiers open on the budget's clock (turns 2/4/6/8/9) or the bots' (rounds 3/6/9/12/14), and either one is what a strong player does.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: The bots' curve is set by hand. In tiers 2-4, bots could afford the next climb in 99-100% of the rounds where they didn't take it, and BG's 2/4/6/8/10 is affordable under our costs. Every break-even price and fixture depends on this clock.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: HARD_CURVE [4,7,9,12,14] (bot_level.gd:20-21, 'tempo beats tiers'); econ_pace2.py.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: Goldfish a fast-tier line (tier 6 by R10-11) and a tempo line, and fight them at R8, R10 and R12. The winner sets the clock for fixtures and costing. Retest the 13-gold last climb.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: Hedgerow's lead is structural (Acorns, Dozey, concentration), so the other tribes should be raised to its level.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: Its lobby wins run through Squire Lollop, a tier-6 board-wide aura that other tribes splash. Its R9 fixture win is a Health breakpoint that an even spread of 5/6s reproduces. The R9 boards have no tier 6, so the lobby data and the fixtures are measuring different stages of the game.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: 70 of 71 Hedgerow lobby wins had Lollop, and 422 of the 568 final boards holding him were other tribes'. Dozey's lift is 0.63. hedgerow_low wins 99.6%; even 5/6s win 96.5%.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: Constructed R9 and R14-16 boards with Lollop and the Committee swapped for plain bodies, and with them splashed onto other tribes' boards. Shift Hedgerow's Health by ±1 to find the cliff.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: Bot lobby rates and the bench's board totals can rank tribes and cards.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: The plain bot values text at 1.5 × tier, climbs on one curve and spends all its gold. The bench adds only base, permanent and tribe stats, so auras, Rings, Eggs, Bellies and fight buffs are missing. Constructed sims will inherit that blind spot if they reuse the same count.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: Fairies were picked in 29 of 3,200 seats and took first in 31% of those. Queen of Elfland sat on 634 non-Fairy boards. bench.gd:383-393 sums combat_spec only. Held Ooze bodies add about 25%.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: Log per-unit stats at the start of combat, held bodies included, in both the bench and the fixtures. Use lobby data only as the owner's occasional sanity check.

owner_hypothesis.claim: If a unit whose double is capped at +8/+8 can overwhelm games, our power budget is far too low (9a).
owner_hypothesis.reason: The budget is too low and too flat: a tier 4-6 body arrives at 0.60-0.74 of the median unit already on the board, and +8/+8 is a quarter of a round-7 board (+40 points of win rate). But Dozey's R9 fixture win is a Health breakpoint: six plain 5/6s win 96.5% too. In lobbies he doesn't predict wins (lift 0.63). Uncapped Dozey (96/94) dominated earlier only against bots that never take answers.

owner_hypothesis.claim: In healthy BG metas nearly every unit ends the game above 100/100 (9a).
owner_hypothesis.reason: Measured: the median BG unit is about 117/117 at turn 12 and 417/417 at turn 14 in the current patch. Even in Sep 2025, the mean unit was about 125/125 at turn 14. Our winners end near 17/17 a unit.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Mid-game units reach 150/150 in many metas (9a).
owner_hypothesis.reason: That size belongs to the carry, not every unit, and only in recent patches. At turn 10 the biggest unit is about 120/120 and the median unit about 40/40 (Nov 2026). A whole turn-10 board was about 300 in Sep 2025, and launch-era BG carries were 30/30-60/60 late.

owner_hypothesis.claim: BG's big numbers come from the compounding effects of economy (9a).
owner_hypothesis.reason: Our income is already BG's: 3 to 10 gold, 3-gold units, 1-gold refresh. The difference is what gold buys: BG turns gold into 2.8 stats at turn 8 and 71 at turn 14, while we stay at 1.4-1.5. That comes from second-order text (25% of BG's pool: 'this game', 'improve', doublers) more than from extra gold.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Our tier power budget may not be steep enough (9a).
owner_hypothesis.reason: Right that new tiers arrive weaker than the board they join. But BG's printed bodies and buffs are small too. Steeper tiers alone give a steeper straight line, not BG's curve.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Large amounts of the design need to be reworked (9a).
owner_hypothesis.reason: 22% of pool units carry a cap or limiter, the budget allows 'linear growth only', only Hedgerow turns gold into stats, and one card in 119 is second-order.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Judge a card by condition and payoff: a T3 2/2 that gains +1/+1 at end of turn matches a 5/5 in three turns and beats it from then on (9a).
owner_hypothesis.reason: On our clock (tier 3 opens around round 6, and winners play to round 19-20) it ends far above a 5/5. Our tools price it wrong: the budget wants it to break even against a plain unit by turn 12, and the bot scores it 8.5 against the 5/5's 14.5, and still won't swap it in after it reaches 5/5.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Most of our effects spread small buffs over many units, and few let stats concentrate (9a).
owner_hypothesis.reason: Concentrating stat payoffs: Birds 4 of 11 (plus 3 partly), Bog 1 of 13, Fairies 1 of 16, Hunters 3 small ones, Oozes 2; Hedgerow has 6 of 13. Ring, Supper and per-fight caps flatten the rest.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Hedgerow's design is fine; its overperformance shows the other tribes are too weak (9a).
owner_hypothesis.reason: Right for Birds (mean place 5.10, 4.9% first), partly right for Bog, and not shown for Fairies (best high-roll board, 77%). Hedgerow's lobby lead runs through Squire Lollop, a board-wide aura that other tribes splash (70 of 71 Hedgerow wins). Its real structural edge, which the others lack, is growth in the Recruit Phase and gold that turns into stats.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Three 10/11s are guaranteed to beat five 10/10s (9a).
owner_hypothesis.reason: Exact under our rules: 5,600 fights over every layout gave one outcome, with one survivor.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Without scam, concentrating stats is always better than spreading them (9a).
owner_hypothesis.reason: Fewer, evenly bigger bodies always win at equal totals. One carry plus small units does not: it wins 0-15% against an even board of the same total, and a carry holding 30% or more of the board loses 9-20 points, because overkill is wasted and every body soaks a whole exchange. Breakpoints decide fights. BG winners are no more concentrated than other boards (biggest unit 33-36% of the board vs 32-35%).

owner_hypothesis.claim: Concentration counts double with units that hold their stats, such as cleave or damage reduction (9a).
owner_hypothesis.reason: Modelled on Dozey: taking 2 less damage adds 24.5 points, immunity while attacking 20.5, a shield 13.3, cleave 11.0. The slice has none of these keywords, which is part of why lone carries underperform here.

owner_hypothesis.claim: A big unit like Dozey value-trades into 2-3 units, so the rest of the board only has to trade one for one (9a).
owner_hypothesis.reason: It holds once the carry clears the enemy's breakpoints: Dozey's 10/16 against a median 4/6 kills 3-4 units. Back-row protection helps too: B3 wins 96.4% against 83.9% in F1.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Our numbers may just be too small in general (9a).
owner_hypothesis.reason: Fights depend only on ratios (the same slope from 42 to 420 stats), so absolute size changes little. Small integers do hurt: one point of Health can swing about 32 points of win rate, and flat effects bite hard. What is too small is growth relative to the board.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Carries at 50/50 by round 12 may still be too small (9c).
owner_hypothesis.reason: Against BG, yes: a turn-12 carry is about 450/450 now and about 125/125 in Sep 2025, and launch-era BG was lower. But fights don't care about absolute size. The real test is feel and the shape of the curve, and nobody has run it.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Rewards must give power so players feel stronger (9c).
owner_hypothesis.reason: Card text adds about 7 stats a round to the whole board, half of a final board is printed bodies, stats per gold fall from 1.41 to 1.05 over the game, and no board in 400 lobbies reached twice the median.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Fun with higher entropy matters more than balance, with tribes in the same order of magnitude (9c).
owner_hypothesis.reason: Our fights are near-deterministic (59 of 66 test pairs fall outside 10-90%), so entropy is low today. A literal 10x bar is already met (first place ranges from 4.9% to 25.3%) while Birds are clearly failing, so the bar needs a metric.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Bots will never be elite, so constructed simulations at turn thresholds are far more reliable (9d).
owner_hypothesis.reason: Right about the bots. But a fixed board measures how strong it is once built, not how often it gets built, and ours are brittle: +1/+1 swings them 22-68 points. Reliable results need rollouts of strong scripted lines through the real shop, then fights between populations of boards.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Feedback loops will make rare runaway games; a top 1% at 10x the average is fine, as long as snowballs aren't common (9d).
owner_hypothesis.reason: That is BG's shape: from turn 8, 13-23% of ordinary boards are at 2x the median, and by turn 14, 3% are at 10x. Bramble has no tail at all: not one board in 400 lobbies reached 2x. Under our damage rule a runaway can't even end games faster, since late damage is mostly the round base.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Bots can't execute greedy, high-APM lines (9d).
owner_hypothesis.reason: Bots had 5+ gold left in under 10% of turns, held a Stash in 19 of 4,475 player-turns, and bought Charcoal Burner in 1 of 240 seats. The saving bot gained +0.05 ± 0.09 places.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Reviewers shouldn't fail good work on power-budget concerns that rarely matter (9d).
owner_hypothesis.reason: The costing reviewer cut 10 of 10 in pass 2 by hand math, won every split with the triage reviewer, and its method has no test for 'too small'.

owner_hypothesis.claim: With scam, one 2.1-billion unit is easier to beat than three 500-million ones; distribution matters (9d).
owner_hypothesis.reason: Without scam the giant wins: it survives four hits and kills one unit per hit. The claim needs answers that can reach it, and ours mostly aim across, can't reach the back row while the front lives, and deal flat amounts. It becomes true once proportional answers that ignore rows exist. Today only Nightshade (−28.5 points on Dozey) and the Wasp come close.

owner_hypothesis.claim: A player who scouts a ghost can adapt to it, but the ghost can't adapt back (9a question).
owner_hypothesis.reason: Ghosts win 7% of fights at 0.8-0.9x the median, where a living board that size wins about 36%. They have no hero power, never change, and are scouted exactly. 817 ghost fights happen with three players alive, which gives someone in the final three a near-bye.

owner_questions.question: How big should late boards get, compared with Battlegrounds eras you know?
options: Launch-era BG (2019-20): carries 30/30-60/60 late, boards in the low hundreds, compounding rare
Sep 2025 BG: about x1.5 a round from round 8, carries about 125/125 at round 12, 4-digit boards only in the end game
Current BG (Nov 2026): about x1.8 a round, 4-5 digit boards, carries about 450/450 at round 12
owner_questions.default_answer: Sep 2025 BG: carries in the low hundreds by round 12, with 4-digit totals only in the end game or in highrolls.
owner_questions.value: Sets how many compounding engines each tribe gets (almost none, one or two, or several plus doublers), whether every flat effect (Bitter, Hex, 3 damage, Sergeant) turns into a proportional one, and how many digits a card face must fit.

owner_questions.question: How long should a winner's game be?
options: 18-20 rounds, as now
15-16 rounds
13-14 rounds, like BG
owner_questions.default_answer: 15-16 rounds.
owner_questions.value: Sets the damage table and Health (now 40 Health, with a round base of 0 to 13), which sets how cheap early losses are and so the price of greed. Together with question 1 it fixes the growth rate: x1.5 a round over the 11 rounds after round 8 we play now is about 90x; over 7 rounds it is about 17x.

owner_questions.question: How often may one player run away with a lobby?
options: Rarely: the round-8 leader wins at most 20% of lobbies, and under 10% of boards reach 2x the round median at rounds 10-12
Like BG: the round-8 leader wins at most 30%, 15-25% of boards reach 2x the median at rounds 10-12, and 10x outliers stay under 1% of games
Swingy: 25-35% of boards at 2x, and the leader wins up to 40%
owner_questions.default_answer: Like BG.
owner_questions.value: This becomes the pass/fail bar for every uncapped engine and for reviewers. Anything inside it ships; anything outside it gets a rate limit or a new answer, not a cap.

owner_questions.question: Should every tribe get a compounding 'this game' engine, or may some tribes win without big stats?
options: Every tribe compounds stats
Every tribe compounds, and two also have a strong route that doesn't rely on stats (answers, width or reserve bodies), like BG's Beetles or Murloc handbuff
Three or four tribes compound; two win mainly through answers, summons or reserves
owner_questions.default_answer: Every tribe compounds, and two also get a strong route that doesn't rely on stats: Bog as the answer tribe, Oozes through their Belly reserves.
owner_questions.value: This is the pass-3 content brief: which tribes get 'this game' engines and doublers, and which get scam and width instead.

owner_questions.question: Should answers be able to reach a carry hidden in the back row?
options: Freely: several 'wherever it stands' answers, like BG's venom
Rarely: a few answers that ignore rows (one neutral, one or two tribes); most aim across or at the front
No: the front row guards the carry, and you have to break it first
owner_questions.default_answer: Rarely.
owner_questions.value: Decides whether uncapped carries are safe and what the answer cards look like. The first option also changes what the back row means: today it is the place a carry hides.

owner_questions.question: How swingy should a single fight be in the mid and late game?
options: As now: near-deterministic (a board at 1.5x the median wins 94%)
Like BG: the side with fewer stats wins about 15-25% of fights
Swingier: 25-35%
owner_questions.default_answer: Like BG.
owner_questions.value: Sets how much variance we add: summons, shields, answers, random targets that ignore rows. Without it, a compounding curve lets a one-round lead decide every fight.

owner_questions.question: When you say tribes should be within the same order of magnitude, what should we measure?
options: First-place rate per tribe between 8% and 20% in lobbies of scripted lines
Each tribe's best common line wins 35-65% against the field at rounds 8, 12 and 16, in fights between populations of constructed boards
Median stats within 2x of each other at each round
owner_questions.default_answer: The second, with the first as a sanity check.
owner_questions.value: This is the pass/fail bar for each tribe pass. Today's first-place spread of 4.9-25.3% already passes a literal 10x, while Birds are clearly failing.

owner_questions.question: Should Squire Lollop and the Standing Committee buff only Hedgerow folk?
options: Hedgerow folk only
Keep them board-wide in Hedgerow
Board-wide, moved to the neutral pool
owner_questions.default_answer: Hedgerow folk only, and the neutral pool gets its own late full-board card.
owner_questions.value: Decides whether Hedgerow is the benchmark the other tribes are raised to. Its bot lead is mostly Lollop (70 of 71 wins), and 422 of the 568 final boards holding him were other tribes'.

missing: Growth rate and game length are one decision, and no map joined them. At Sep 2025 BG's rate (x1.5 a round from round 8), our 20-round games end about 90x above round 8, which is current-BG numbers. BG's turns 8 to 14 give about 14x.

No map asked what compounding does inside our near-deterministic combat. +10% stats is worth about 15 points at any scale, and a board at 1.5x the median wins 94%. An exponential curve then makes a one-round lead decisive. The rework needs a variance budget measured as the share of fights the smaller board wins (BG: 14-26%).

No map proposed a way to measure how often a board happens without bots. Constructed sims the rework needs, and what each measures: (1) a distribution grid: boards with equal totals (seven even units, five big, three big, BG's carry with a third of the stats, an all-in carry) at R6/9/12/16 sizes, with and without one answer and each stat-holding keyword; it measures what actually wins fights. (2) An answer matrix: each answer against carry boards at R12 and R16, carry in B3 and in front, scouted and blind; it measures each answer's swing. (3) Goldfish rollouts: 2-3 strong scripted lines per tribe through the real shop and pool, 500+ seeds; they measure the spread of boards by round, stats per gold, the tail, and tier and triple timing. (4) Population round robins of rollout boards at R8, R12 and R16; they measure each line's win rate against the field, how win rate follows the stat ratio, and how often the smaller board wins. (5) Cap removal and one uncapped 'this game' engine per tribe, run inside (3) and (4); they measure tail growth and whether answers still win 30%+. (6) Scripted-line lobbies with the real damage rule; they measure how often the round-8 leader wins, the share of winners below the median at round 8, game length and the greed line's Health.

Harvest Supper's tribe bonus (rule 5.2.9) is the pool's only 'this game' layer: it reaches every unit of the tribe you will ever own, in hand, in Bellies and away. It is capped at +3/+3. Maps listed it as one cap among many, not as the cheapest system-level lever, BG's Undead/Beast 'this game' pattern, open to every tribe at once.
Tavern spells are in the shop but never grow. In current BG a large share of late growth runs through text that improves spells. That is a ready second-order channel nobody proposed.

The feedback loops in our own rules were never listed or modelled: Early Spoils (1 gold a win in rounds 1-4), the triple reward's discover from the tier above, golden text doubling a growth rate (a golden engine compounds twice as fast), and Last Stand as the only rubber band. Pace data found that early wins predict place even at equal board size, and nobody explained why.

The slice has no stat-holding keywords and no trample: no shield, Reborn, cleave, windfury, venom or damage reduction. The owner's 'doubly' point, and the trample idea he liked on 2 Nov, depend on them; modelled on a carry they add 11-25 points.
No constructed boards exist past R9, and none include tier 6. The late game, where the curve gap opens, is untested by fixtures.

The strong-player reference curve for fixtures (tier, gold and triples by turn) can be measured from the 129 parsed BG replays and adapted to our costs. So the process map's question to the owner about it can be dropped.
Whether 4-5 digit numbers stay readable on the 4-3 board at phone size is untested, and it limits how far the scale can go.

critics.verdict: The game is flat by construction, and every check we ran was relative (card against a plain unit, tribe against tribe, bot against bot), so nothing flagged it. Engines are priced to break even with a plain body and capped per turn, so investing never pays off. Gold is the same for everyone and saving earns nothing. Most payoffs last one fight, so they reset and don't show in the shop. Boards grow 40% a turn at R5 and 7% at R16, against Battlegrounds' 55-95% from turn 8: the late game gives the smallest rewards when the stakes are highest, and there are no highrolls to chase. Bot data can't see this. The owner's claims mostly hold, with two corrections under our rules: the economy-to-tempo loop has almost nothing to run on yet, so today's risk is no snowballs; and with no timer, many-action lines are open to any patient human, so the human tail may be fatter than Battlegrounds'. The rework needs sims scored against a sampled field of reachable boards: curve shape, invest against tempo, greed against tempo, carry against answers. Playtests against bots shouldn't count as snowball evidence.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: Bot lobbies measure tribe strength, card strength and how often snowballs happen.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: The bar measures the bot. Bots rate card text at 1.5 x tier, all follow one climb curve, spend all their gold, never buy against the scout and never buy answers. That hides engines, answers and greed lines, which are what the rework is about.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: Fairies picked by 0.9% of seats but first in 31% of them. Birds' first rate moved from 13.5% to 4.9% between runs. Changeling and Ichneumon Wasp were on 0 of 3,200 final boards. Gold left was 5 or more in under 10% of turns. No board ever reached 2x the lobby median in 400 lobbies.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: Stop tuning to lobby results. Build a constructed-field harness (S0). For R6, R9, R12 and R15, take 60-100 boards from seeded shop sequences: several lines per tribe, on average, high and low rolls. Score each candidate by its win rate against the whole field, sides swapped, with combat-start stats logged per unit. Run lobbies only as a sanity check every few passes.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: Capping growth per tier and pricing engines to break even with a plain unit by turn 12 is fair.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: It makes investing pointless. An engine can never end up much better than a plain body. So the arc the owner describes (worse now, level in 3 turns, better every turn after) is ruled out by construction.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: The owner's own T3 2/2 that gains +1/+1 at End of Turn is over budget until Tier 4. The T3 cap is 1.7 SP a turn and the card makes 2 (power-budget.md:205). 7 of the 10 pass 2 cuts were for growth over the caps. Our T4-6 payoffs give about 3 SP a turn, against 32 in Battlegrounds. A capped payoff adds about 2% of the board a turn.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: Invest-against-tempo sim (S2). For each engine at its real opening round, on the same seed, buy either the engine or the best tempo buy. Fight both against the field 0 to 5 turns later. Lift the caps on 2-3 engines per tribe. Target: behind at once, level after 2-3 turns, clearly ahead after that.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: Our numbers are too small, so scaling them up fixes the game.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: Plain combat only cares about ratios. Multiplying every stat by k changes nothing but rounding. What is missing is growth relative to the board, and a tail. Scaling up helps only on the side: finer tuning steps and smaller flat effects.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: +10% stats moves win rate by about 15 pp at every scale (scale.txt). Board growth per round falls from 40% at R5 to 16% at R10 and 7% at R16. Battlegrounds grows by x1.5-1.9 a turn from turn 8 to 14. 25% of Battlegrounds' pool is compounding text; Bramble has one such card (Fairy Monarch).
wrong_assumptions.try_first: Curve-shape sim (S1). Run 200 seeds per tribe on a scripted strong line, with one uncapped 'this game' engine per tribe. Record board power at p50, p90 and p99 for R8, R11 and R14, the share of boards at 2x the median or more, and the biggest unit's share. Compare these with the target curve. Do the x4 rescale in the same pass for finer steps, not as the fix.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: Board stat totals measure strength.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: Breakpoints and how stats are spread decide fights. The totals we log also leave out the power that wins.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: The biggest board in a lobby wins only 76-79% of its fights, and every board between 0.65x and 0.95x the median wins 35-39%. The two most common cards on winning boards (Lollop, Isegrim) give combat-only buffs that aren't logged, and Eggs, Rings and Belly bodies are left out too. In Battlegrounds the side with fewer stats won 14-26% of fights.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: Score every board by its win rate against the field, never by SP. Log each unit's stats at the start of combat (after auras, held bodies included) and the biggest unit's share of the board.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: Fixed R9 boards at equal spend are a fair benchmark.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: Equal spend, one growth layer, one author and one round strip out what the owner cares about: economy lines, compounding, roll luck and the late game. At small numbers combat is nearly deterministic, so each pair becomes a test of where breakpoints fall.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: 59 of 66 plain pairs fall outside 10-90%. +1/+1 on every unit moves boards by 0-68 pp. There is no T6. All 12 boards were built by one hand from gold ledgers.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: Replace single pairs with the field (S0). Report win rate along stat curves (+5%, +10%, +20%), not after a single +1/+1. Add boards with different spend at the same round (greed against tempo). Run R12 and R15 as well as R9. Build boards from seeded shops so they are reachable, not from hand ledgers.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: Economy is a real decision layer: banking, interest, gold engines, and the owner's economy-to-tempo loop.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: Gold is the same for everyone and saving pays nothing, so the choice to greed is hollow. The loop the owner describes has nothing to run on.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: Every tribe spends 9.7-10.1 gold a round, and nothing raises income above 10. The median most anyone banks in a game is 3. The interest hero places last (5.53). The rising refresh price never fired in 48,773 turns. Late gold buys 0.75-0.9 stats. Playtest tally row 12 says saving gold is a trap. From R12 a loss costs 11-13 Health, so a leader can't afford to greed just when the lead would allow it.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: Greed-against-tempo sim (S3). On the same seeds, run a tempo line against an economy line (bank for a big climb, hold Acorns, climb fast). Measure Health lost by R8 (from the calibrated Health model and win rates against the field), board power at R11 and R14, and how often the greed line ends ahead. This shows whether an economy lead can become a tempo lead at all.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: Combat-only payoffs are a fair main reward for a tribe.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: The player can't see them while recruiting, they reset after every fight and they never build up. They don't feel like progress.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: 10 of 13 Hunter stat payoffs and 9 of 13 Bog ones last one fight only. Costing moved Lollop, Laird and Elder Ooze to combat-only to fit under the caps. T5-6 bodies arrive at 0.6x the size of the units already on the board, so tier-ups look like downgrades in the shop.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: Count each tribe's share of permanent payoffs that show in the shop, and set a floor of about half. Show combat-start stats in the shop. Then run S2 on the converted payoffs.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: Answers aimed at the unit 'across' are real answers to a carry.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: They land only when the two layouts line up, and the carry's owner chooses its slot after seeing the scout. They are also untested: bots never buy them, so no playtester has met one.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: Changeling and Wasp were on 0 of 3,200 final boards. The slice has no poison, no destroy and no 'attacks the biggest'. In the model, Nightshade on Dozey's board costs it 28.5 pp. The scout shows the opponent's board from the last round.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: Carry-against-answer sim (S4). Fight each tribe's best R11 and R14 carry board against field boards holding 0, 1 and 2 answers, with the carry's owner re-placing after the scout (sampled layouts). Then add one answer that targets the biggest enemy and compare. Target: a common board with one answer beats the carry about 30% of the time or more.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: Human playtests against bots can judge fun and how often snowballs happen.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: The human has no timer, reads bots that pin their carries in place, never faces an answer and never faces a greedy opponent. After the rework a human will snowball against linear bots in most games. That will look like the common snowball the owner fears, but it is the mismatch. Under tally rule E it would bring the caps straight back.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: Tally row 3 ('one huge unit decides', 11 reports) became caps, in games where bots never bought an answer. Bots use the scout only for placement. Ghosts lose 93.5% of their fights.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: Before the rework lands, count snowball and dominance reports only when a constructed sim reproduces them. Give playtests a 'strong field' mode: each round's opponent comes from that round's constructed field, so the human meets strong boards and answers.

wrong_assumptions.assumption: Scope reviews per step, a costing veto and the tally rule keep the whole game on course.
wrong_assumptions.why_wrong: Every check was relative: card against a plain unit, tribe against tribe, bot against bot. Nothing compared the game with a reference game or a feel target. So the process could balance a uniformly flat game and call that a success.
wrong_assumptions.evidence: At least 19 caps or limiters were added in 3 days; 22% of units now carry one, against about 5% in Battlegrounds. Costing won 10 of 10 cuts and every split, with no sims and no 'too small' test. The orchestrator set the 13/13-by-turn-12 scale target on 6 Nov, and nobody tested it for feel. Scope reviewers see one commit range at a time.
wrong_assumptions.try_first: Make the pass bar absolute: the S1 curve against the owner's target, plus bars from S2 to S4. Give the costing reviewer sims through Sol and make it advise only, with a 'too small' check. Run a whole-game critic every pass that reads all new caps and the curve.

owner_hypothesis.claim: If Dozey's capped growth is enough to overwhelm a game, the power budget is far too low across the board.
owner_hypothesis.reason: The other tribes' payoffs are far too small: about 3 SP a turn at T4-6, against 32 in Battlegrounds. But Dozey's edge is his size against a small field (10/16 against a median 4/6 at R9), and an even board with 6 Health on every unit wins as often (96.5% against 95.7%). In bot lobbies Dozey boards place worse. Squire Lollop drives Hedgerow's wins.

owner_hypothesis.claim: In healthy Battlegrounds metas nearly every unit ends over 100/100, and carries reach 150/150 mid-game.
owner_hypothesis.reason: Current patch: the median unit is about 117/117 at turn 12, and the median biggest unit is 240 stats at turn 10 and 897 at turn 12. Even in the tamest recent era (Sep 2025) units reach about 125/125 by turn 14. Ours are about 10/10 at R12 and 17/17 at the end.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Our tier power budget isn't steep enough.
owner_hypothesis.reason: Battlegrounds' printed bodies and buffs are small too (+2 to +6 per buff). Its scale comes from compounding text: 25% of its pool against 1 Bramble card. What we lack is steep payoff growth, not steeper bodies. Still, T5-6 bodies arrive at 0.6x the units already on the board, which makes tier-ups feel like downgrades.

owner_hypothesis.claim: A T3 2/2 that gains +1/+1 at End of Turn costs about the same as a 5/5 and is better after 3 turns.
owner_hypothesis.reason: The principle is right, but our method rules that card over budget until Tier 4. The T3 growth cap is 1.7 SP a turn and the card makes 2 (power-budget.md:205). The bot values it at 8.5 against the 5/5's 14.5 and replaces it even after it reaches 5/5. Both the method and the bot must change.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Judge every card by its condition, its payoff and what it enables.
owner_hypothesis.reason: Our method prices each card alone, gives no value for enabling other cards, and has no test for a payoff that is too small.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Hedgerow is fine; its overperformance shows the other tribes are too weak.
owner_hypothesis.reason: Right for Birds, which are last on every measure. Partly right for Bog. Not shown for Fairies, whose high-roll board is the best at 77%. Hedgerow's lobby lead is mostly Squire Lollop, a full-board aura any tribe can run: 70 of 71 Hedgerow wins had it, and Hedgerow players without Lollop or Committee place 5.99 on average. Bots barely play its Acorn engine, though Dozey wins the constructed low roll (99.6%).

owner_hypothesis.claim: Three 10/11s always beat five 10/10s.
owner_hypothesis.reason: Exact under our rules: 5,600 fights across every placement gave one outcome, with one survivor.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Without scam, concentrating stats is always better than spreading them.
owner_hypothesis.reason: At equal totals, fewer and bigger bodies win every time, for boards of two or more units. One carry with small units around it loses: it needs about 1.37x the stats, and a lone carry wins or loses on Last Blow parity. On real R9 boards, a buff spread across the board does as well as the same buff on one unit (68.9% against 68.1%). Our damage also counts survivors, so concentrated wins deal less damage.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Units that hold their stats (hit an extra unit, take less damage) make concentration doubly strong.
owner_hypothesis.reason: In the plain combat model, giving Dozey damage reduction adds 24.5 pp, immunity while attacking adds 20.5 and cleave adds 11. Not yet run in the engine, and the slice has almost no such effects.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Most effects spread small buffs, so a big unit value-trades 2-3 enemies and the rest of the board only needs to trade 1-for-1.
owner_hypothesis.reason: Few payoffs concentrate stats: 4 of 11 in Birds (some only partly), 1 of 13 in Bog, 1 of 16 in Fairies, 6 of 13 in Hedgerow. Dozey at 10/16 against 4/6 units kills 3-4 of them. The mechanism is breakpoints: he one-shots each enemy and survives its hit.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Our numbers may just be too small in general.
owner_hypothesis.reason: Plain combat cares only about ratios, so multiplying every stat changes nothing but rounding. What is too small is growth relative to the board (40% a turn at R5, 7% at R16) and the tail (no board ever reached 2x the median). A bigger scale helps on the side: +1/+1 moves fixed fights 30 pp now and 9 pp at 4x, and flat effects shrink.

owner_hypothesis.claim: The active player adapts to a ghost that can't adapt back.
owner_hypothesis.reason: Ghosts lose 93.5% of their fights. A ghost at 0.8-0.9x the median wins 7%, where a live board that size wins about 36%. The scout of a ghost shows its exact board, and the ghost has no hero power. 817 ghost fights come with three players left. Ghost fights are only 3% of all fights, and async play (rulebook 2.1.4) would replace ghosts.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Carries at 50/50 by R12 may still be too small.
owner_hypothesis.reason: Even in the tamest recent Battlegrounds era the average board at turn 12 is 759 stats (about 54/54 a unit), with carries above that. Now the median biggest unit at turn 12 has 897 stats. Whether a given size makes a good game is untested.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Rewards always give power; players must feel stronger.
owner_hypothesis.reason: Our rules fail it. A capped payoff adds about 2% of the board a turn, and board growth per turn falls from 40% to 7%. Most payoffs last one fight and don't show in the shop. T5-6 bodies arrive smaller than the units they join.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Bots will never be elite; constructed sims at turn thresholds should count for far more than bot play.
owner_hypothesis.reason: Bots rate text at 1.5 x tier, follow one climb curve, never save and never buy answers. One caution: our only constructed bench (R9) was built by one agent at equal spend and gives results near 0% or 100%. The new sims need a sampled field and reachable boards.

owner_hypothesis.claim: An economy lead becomes a tempo lead that lets the leader greed safely; such snowballs will happen, and that's fine if they're rare.
owner_hypothesis.reason: Today the loop has almost nothing to run on. Every tribe spends about 10 gold a round, nothing raises income, and saving pays nothing (the median most anyone banks is 3). From R12 a loss costs 11-13 Health, so a leader can't afford to greed. Only Acorns, Early Spoils and triples compound. Today's risk is no snowballs at all. After the rework, measure it with the greed-against-tempo sim.

owner_hypothesis.claim: A top 1% at 10x the average is fine; the shape of the curve is what matters.
owner_hypothesis.reason: This matches Battlegrounds: from turn 8, 13-23% of ordinary boards are at least 2x the median, and the top tenth of the top 0.4% of games reach 7-18x. In 400 Bramble bot lobbies no board reached 2x. The curve-shape sim can test it.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Bots can't execute many-action lines (Tethys, Proud Privateer, APM Undead).
owner_hypothesis.reason: True for bots. But Bramble has no recruit timer (rulebook 3.1.2), so speed doesn't limit people. Any patient player can run a many-action line, and only the rising refresh price bounds it; bots never reached it. The gap that remains is planning, so the human tail may be fatter than Battlegrounds' for the same content.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Reviewers shouldn't fail good work on power-budget concerns that come up rarely.
owner_hypothesis.reason: Costing cut 10 of 10 pass 2 items by hand math, 7 of them for growth over the caps, and won every split. At least 19 caps were added in 3 days. The method has no 'too small' test.

owner_hypothesis.claim: Distribution beats total: one huge unit is easier to beat than three big ones.
owner_hypothesis.reason: Under our rules, one answer that ignores size (Nightshade, Bufo's halving, Changeling, Wasp) handles one carry; three carries need three. But our answers mostly hit the unit across, so they land by layout luck. There is no poison or destroy. Bots never play Changeling or Wasp (0 of 3,200 boards), so nobody has tested them.

owner_questions.question: What curve should a strong (not elite) player's board follow, and when should the game end?
options: Battlegrounds, Sep 2025: about x1.5 a turn from R8; median board about 300 at R10, 750 at R12, 1,750 at R14
Battlegrounds now: about x1.9 a turn; about 700, 2,600 and 8,000
A steeper straight line: about 3x today (around 400 at R12), no compounding
owner_questions.default_answer: The Sep 2025 shape, with Battlegrounds' tail: about 15-20% of boards at 2x the median from R10, the top 1% up to 10x, and winners done by R14-16.
owner_questions.value: Sets the growth rates, gold value and payoff sizes in every tribe, the pass bar for the curve-shape sim, and the Health clock. Today winners play 19.5 rounds.

owner_questions.question: Where should compounding come from?
options: Stats: 'this game' counters and payoffs that scale; income stays flat at 10
Gold: income raises, interest and gold engines that feed stat buys
Both: mostly stats, plus one or two cards per tribe that raise gold or pay per gold spent
owner_questions.default_answer: Both, mostly stats.
owner_questions.value: Decides whether the economy layer (income cap, banking, interest hero, spell rates) is reworked or only the content. With flat gold, your economy-to-tempo loop has nothing to run on.

owner_questions.question: Should every tribe have a route to one big carry it grows and protects, or should some tribes win wide or with answers?
options: Every tribe gets one carry route and one way to hold stats (shield, damage reduction)
Four tall tribes; two win wide or with answers, as Beetles and Murlocs do in Battlegrounds
Carries come only from neutral cards
owner_questions.default_answer: Every tribe gets a carry route. Bog and Oozes also get a strong non-carry route (answers for Bog, width for Oozes).
owner_questions.value: Sets the pass-3 brief for all six tribes. Today only Hedgerow has a carry the player picks and grows.

owner_questions.question: Must every tribe's main payoffs be permanent growth you can see in the shop, or can a tribe live on fight-only power?
options: Every tribe's main payoffs are permanent; fight-only text is for answers and tempo
Allow one fight-only tribe (Hunters) if its fight numbers are big and shown before the fight
Keep today's mix
owner_questions.default_answer: Every tribe's main payoffs are permanent.
owner_questions.value: Decides how much of Hunters (10 of 13 payoffs fight-only) and Bog (9 of 13) is rewritten, and whether the shop shows combat-start stats.

owner_questions.question: Should answers to a big unit aim at it, or keep hitting the unit across, so that beating a carry is a placement guess?
options: Aimed: poison-like, 'the biggest enemy', percentage damage
Across: a mind game read from the scout
A mix: a few aimed answers in the neutral pool; tribal answers stay across
owner_questions.default_answer: A mix.
owner_questions.value: Decides whether placement is a real decision layer, how big carries may grow without caps, and which answer cards are rewritten.

owner_questions.question: Which lobby should the fundamentals serve, given there is no timer?
options: The live 8-player lobby with bots (today's build); async later
Async recorded runs (rulebook 2.1.4): tune for that now
Live, plus a cap on shops or actions a turn (Galaxy stops at 30 shops)
owner_questions.default_answer: The live lobby for now, with the refresh price as the only brake until sims show many-action lines dominate. Spend nothing on fixing ghosts.
owner_questions.value: Decides whether ghosts, Last Stand and scouting are fixed now, and how wide the human skill tail gets. With no timer, many-action lines are open to any patient player.

owner_questions.question: Should a crushing late win hurt more than a narrow one?
options: Keep: from R12 the round base is most of the damage (survivors are 11-16% of a loss)
From R10 each survivor deals 2
Survivors deal damage by their tier, as in Battlegrounds
owner_questions.default_answer: From R10 each survivor deals 2; then re-check pace.
owner_questions.value: Decides whether concentrated and blowout boards earn anything in Health, and moves the game-length target.

owner_questions.question: Will you check a dozen constructed boards (R6, R9, R12, R15; typical and high roll) as what a strong player would have at that point?
options: Yes, about 10 minutes
Only give a strong player's tier and triple timeline under our costs
No: trust hindsight-search lines on seeded shops
owner_questions.default_answer: No. Use hindsight-search lines as the upper bound and scripted lines as typical play.
owner_questions.value: Sets how much weight the sims carry. All 12 of today's benchmark boards were built by one agent.

missing: The target game is async with no timer (rulebook 2.1.4 and 3.1.2), and the ideation build has no timer either. Every map analysed a live Battlegrounds lobby. Without a timer, nothing limits how many actions a turn takes, and that limit is what keeps Battlegrounds' many-action lines rare. So the human skill tail could be fatter than Battlegrounds' for the same content. Async play also needs new rules for scouting and the ghost (2.1.5 is open).

No map set out the arc by phase. Early (R1-4): a loss costs 0-1 Health and a win pays 1 gold, so the player wants tempo and has few real choices (tally row 9). Mid (R5-11): climbs follow hand-set bot curves, new-tier bodies arrive below the board average, and triples are the main reward. Late (R12+): any loss costs 11-13, the margin barely counts, payoffs add about 2% a turn and T6 bodies are 0.6x the board's units, so the player wants not to lose and to find goldens. No phase has a 'this is my spike turn' decision.

Felt reward per turn: board growth as a share of the board falls from 40% at R5 to 7% at R16, while Battlegrounds grows 55-95% a turn from turn 8. No map tied this to motivation. Our late game gives the smallest jumps when the stakes are highest.

Visibility: no map checked what the player sees while recruiting. Combat-only buffs, Eggs fighting at half stats and units held in Bellies don't show in the shop, so the player can neither feel nor plan that power. Breakpoints are hidden arithmetic: at R9, one point changes the result for 26-33% of unit pairs.

Nobody re-read the playtest tally for the bot mismatch. Row 3 ('one huge unit decides', 11 reports) came from games where bots never bought an answer. Row 12 ('saving gold is a trap') and row 9 ('rounds 1-4 scripted') are decision-quality signals that match the economy data, yet they were treated as card fixes.

No map said what constructed boards should fight, or how to make them a strong player's boards. Proposal: build boards on seeded shop sequences so they are reachable. Scripted lines give typical play, a hindsight search over buys on the same seed gives the elite upper bound, and bots give the floor. Score every board against the whole field for its round, sides swapped, along stat curves (+5%, +10%, +20%) rather than a single +1/+1.

Commit against pivot: 37% of seats end with no tribe, and Lollop is on 422 non-Hedgerow boards. No map measured whether committing to a tribe pays. Sim: a committed tribal board against an any-tribe board of the strongest cards, at the same gold, at R11 and R14. Flat auras (Lollop +2/+2, Supper +3/+3) shrink relative to the board once growth compounds, so a Lollop fix made before the rescale may be wasted.

Tier-up value: no sim tested whether climbing feels like progress. Sim: at R9, R12 and R14, compare climbing and buying a new-tier card against staying and rolling, scored against the field 1-3 turns later.

Comebacks: a player wins 60% of fights after a win and 41% after a loss, and board size relative to the lobby correlates 0.76-0.80 between rounds two apart. Nobody looked at the way back for a player who is behind at R8 (a pivot, answers, Last Stand), which is half the curve shape. The curve sims should report how often a board below the median at R8 finishes in the top 2.

Highrolls: triples are the only highroll players reach (winners hold 3.58 goldens, 8th place 1.05), and the buy is obvious, so the spike comes from shop luck rather than a decision. Goldens double effects too. Once engines compound, a golden engine doubles its rate and may drive snowballs. Untested.

Skill expression: no map measured how much a better decision gains (climb or buy, roll or save, placement against the scout). Combat is nearly deterministic and the scout shows the opponent's last board. So against bots that keep their carry in one slot, placement is close to solved; against people it is a guess. Without these numbers we can't say where skill shows.
